utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because we're in a new courtroom again, Mr. Krnojelac, I should ask you: Are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone isn't on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can hear and I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you have any trouble, let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. I just have problems with my spectacles again, because this morning when they put that flak jacket on, somehow they broke, so I'll try to make good use of them today. But thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Krnojelac. I wish you the best of luck in getting your glasses fixed. I apologise for not having reminded you yesterday that we were being moved out of number 1 courtroom so that the Appeals Chamber could take precedence. And I do remind you now that we will be sitting slightly different afternoon hours. We will be adjourning at the lunch hour until 3.00 and we'll then sit through to 4.30. That is because of a judgement which Judge Mumba and I are involved in which is being delivered at 2.00. Right. Well, now, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. THE WITNESS EKREM ZEKOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Kuo: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zekovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're having some problems with the microphones here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, yesterday you mentioned three people whom you saw taken out of the KP Dom on a so-called exchange, and one of the people that you mentioned by name was Ramo Dzendusic. Could you tell us a little bit more about him? What kind of work did he do and what else did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramo Dzendusic is a relative of mine. He worked as a clerk at the military office before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from the village of Hum. That's 20 kilometres out of Foca, to the south, actually, upstream, if you look at the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zekovic. Was there ever an incident in September of 1992 when people were taken out and told they would pick plums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Two groups were taken, two groups that were told they were going to pick plums. Some people's names were called out from a list. Individuals volunteered, wanting to get out. Some were discreetly told by the guards like, "That's not for you," and at that time they held it against those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, they held it against those people? Held what against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People wanted to get out. They knew that getting out meant that they would get more food, and the very fact that they were supposed to go out and pick plums meant that, after all that time, they would manage to eat plums, at least, to their hearts' content. Secondly, staying indoors all the time, without doing anything, that's very difficult; it's tormenting. Therefore, people felt it was necessary to go out, to work, to move about. Time passes more quickly that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that how you felt about the work you were doing? Did you volunteer or were you forced to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a volunteer. My friend, Uzeir Hadzalic, who was in Room 13 opposite my room, asked me one day whether I'd like to go out and work. We had this well-developed system of communication, a sign language. In that way, we conveyed information to one another. Of course, I said yes immediately. That meant an additional meal, no matter how small. It was very important nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the plum pickers, do you know the names of any people who were taken out to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these people's names were called out for plum picking, I was at the metal workshop. I was not in the room. After that, people told me about this. I know many people who were taken away. Right now, if necessary, I can look at some lists that I have here, but two groups were taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on we got to know what we had assumed all along. These people were taken out to military positions. They were digging trenches in the area towards Gorazde. Later on, we received some information to the effect that some of them were seen killed above Ustikolina. In that zone, a few years later, I don't know exactly how many years later, a mass grave was found as well. As far as I know, seven corpses were found there. I think that only two were identified, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the identity of two of those corpses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Halid Konjo and Murat Crneta, as far as I heard. I and the person who is called FWS-210 in this case, outside the KP Dom, we heard that he saw Rasim Kajgana there at that locality, that he had been killed there. Rasim Kajgana was in the same room that I was in. He was a butcher from Foca. He had his own shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who saw Rasim Kajgana's body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb, a Serb who was good friends with that friend of mine whom I just mentioned. I don't know him. Before the war, he was also on good terms with this Rasim. They had a cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was this information conveyed to you or to 210? Was it while you were still at KP Dom or after you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while we were still at the KP Dom. Once when we went to the hospital, that is to say outside the compound, we met people. We would talk and that's how we obtained information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that people had been taken to dig trenches? Was that in the same manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, yet another group was taken late in the autumn. It was already wintertime. They were taken outside the camp and they returned, each and every one of them. They were at that locality, nearby. While they were there, they heard from the soldiers and the local people that many people were killed there, people who had been brought there in the previous groups, to work there, to dig trenches. They were returned to the camp in 1993, that was after the New Year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the second group you mean that was returned in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was a separate group. It was taken much later, much, much later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the location was? You said where people learned from the locals that a group had been taken there to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with that area and I don't know the names of these villages and things like that but it's above Ustikolina, near Previla. Zebina Suma is nearby and that's where the positions were facing Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second group that you mentioned, the one that was taken late in the autumn to that location, where they also there to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as we know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long they were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the Court's permission, I would like to refer to Exhibit P55, which is Schedule C, and rather than showing that to the witness, I'll read some names out and perhaps we will move smoothly that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whichever way you find easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, I'd like to ask you about a few individuals, and I'll tell you their names and you can tell us whether you know what happened, whether you know that person and whether you know what happened to that person at KP Dom. Person C-6, Juso Dzamalja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that person from before the war, for many years. He was a salesperson. I know that he committed suicide in the solitary confinement cell after terrible torture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: C-7, Kemal Dzelilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that person too from before the war. He was a teacher at the high school. He was taken out several times, interrogated allegedly, and beaten up. One evening, he was taken away and he's never been seen since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that this person was beaten up? Did you see injuries or did you learn of -- did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who were in the same room with him told me about it. I saw him taken out a few times and I saw that he could barely move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: C-8, Ramo Dzendusic, you already mentioned that you saw him taken out in part of the groups for the so-called exchanges. Did you ever see him beaten? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him being beaten as he was taken out. His hands were tied on the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: C-9 is Adil Granov. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I knew him personally. We worked in the same company. He was an engineer. He was detained and interrogated on the suspicion that he had travelled abroad before the war, allegedly for signing contracts in order to obtain weapons. Allegedly he went to Germany. For a while he was held in an area in the old building, the old wing of the building, underneath the staircase, where there was a pantry, where brooms and brushes were kept. He was taken out several times and beaten badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "in the old building," are you referring to the administrative building, the old part of the administrative building, or in the detainees' quarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's part of the prison. It's a part that was made earlier, during the days of Austro-Hungary, and there was another wing that was added on later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could show us on Exhibit P6, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is the old part of the prison that I talked about and this is this new part of the prison. Viewed from the outside, they're almost identical. The entrance is about here, and this area was on the ground floor as soon as you'd enter, underneath the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness has indicated as the building that he is referring to as the old building, what is marked on the Exhibit P6 as building 1, where the detainees were kept. I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P6/2, which is a close-up picture that has some more detail, and perhaps he can show us on that diagram the room that he's referring to. This is the ground floor of the prisoners' quarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance into the building. However, this staircase has not been drawn properly. They go from this side and then up here, whereas here it's been drawn this way. This is where the room was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness is indicating where the stairs are drawn in on building number 1, and I believe he was indicating the error in the drawing was just the direction of the staircase. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same as far as the new wing of the building is concerned. Again, there's been a mistake in the way the stairs have been drawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And the new wing is indicated on the exhibit as building 2 of the prisoners' quarters. Thank you very much. Was that room under the stair used normally for isolation or for keeping detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long Adil Granov was kept in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long, but I know it was several days, between 7 and 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Granov eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taken away like the others, and there has been no trace of him since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number C-10, Nail Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him too. He was down there in 11 -- 13. He was an older man, a taxi driver before the war, from Cohodar Mahala. He was taken out several times and beaten up. One evening they came, they called out his name, took him out of the room, and he never returned. As he went out, he waved goodbye to the men. He knew he would never come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he was beaten several times. Did you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him many times. I saw him a few times in passing as we were going to have lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those times, did you see injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right hand of his head there were signs of beating. He had bruises there and he could hardly move, and he could hardly use his right hand. People who were in the same room with him, that's a person who worked with me, Uzeir Hadzalic, he told me that several times he could not even go to the restaurant for lunch or dinner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Mr. Hodzic could not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Nail Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mate Ivancic, that's C-11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally from before the war. He was my next-door neighbour. When the war broke out, we were together in the same street. One day my Serb neighbours asked me something like what was Mate like, and I said, "Well, why do you ask? A good man, normal." And they were just shaking their heads. Then they arrested him. I wasn't present, so I don't know the exact location. And they took him to the KP Dom. I had contact with him a few times at the KP Dom. We talked, because the windows of our respective rooms were at the same corner. And during the first few months there was no light; there were no lights in the KP Dom in the evening. He told me that he was taken out and beaten several times. He said that the Serbs had suspected him of having been in Croatia before and, as they put it, that he took part in the slaughter of Serbs. However, I know that he had a passport that proved that he was in Germany, that he was working there temporarily. I knew that as well. But -- and he kept showing this passport but to no avail. One evening, he was taken out, he knew what would happen to him. He left his watch to one of the men who was in the same room with him so if anybody survived, that person should give his watch to his son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Mr. Ivancic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was suspected of participating in the war in Croatia. Was he ever beaten for that reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. He was beaten. They asked him to confess that he had taken part in the aggression, or rather, in the massacre of the Serbs, which is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, signs of beatings. He didn't have any very visible signs on his face, like wounds and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person C-15 is Mustafa Kuloglija, and you've mentioned him already as being one of the people who was beaten one evening when you heard gunshots. Did you know whether he was beaten on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A few times before that he was taken out for interrogation. He thought that that was because he had had a conflict before the war with a Serb who had attacked him, drunk, and that that's why he was beaten so terribly and killed ultimately. I personally knew him. He was a friend of mine. He told me about this incident when it occurred, before the war, a month or two earlier, I don't know exactly. This Serb attacked him, provoked him, whatever, and allegedly he hit him once, and they said that they would take their revenge because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether that Serb beat him at the KP Dom, or others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not tell me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could I ask the Usher, please, to move the ELMO because the position, it's blocking my view of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Person C-17 is Krunoslav Marinovic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally too from before the war in Foca. He had his TV repair shop. He had -- the shop was his own. And I was his wife's friend; that is, we went to school together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same thing as to Mate Ivancic, the same. He was not charged with having been in Croatia, but he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he also beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They beat him several times, oh, yes, surely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you this and did you see injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw injuries on him and once he told me himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One evening he was called out and he left and did not come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: C-19 on the list is Nurko Nisic. You've described the one incident with regard to him. Were there other times when Mr. Nisic was taken out and beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think that he was taken for interrogation before that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that for sure but I assume -- I assume he was -- I mean, seeing that he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number C-20 is Habid Ramovic. Did you know him and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- no, it's Abid Ramovic, no, no. Abid Ramovic was a policeman, and he was killed in the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's -- the Abid Ramovic that you mentioned was not at KP Dom, Abid Ramovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he had some namesakes. Maybe there were several people called that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Listed at Schedule C, number 21 is Husein Rikalo, at 22 is Mithat Rikalo, and at 23 is Zaim Rikalo. Did you know any of those three Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know those people by sight. They were not in my room. They were in a different wing of the building. I know they were taken for interrogation several times, and I also know that one evening, two of those Rikalos were called out, but I don't know their first names. I also -- I only knew that they were brothers. And they stood by the gate for some three or four minutes and then they were taken in, into that passage, into that hallway, and that same moment, terrible screams and terrible cries started, and blows, and they beat them for about one hour. I don't know what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number C-25 is Kemal Tulek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he spent a long time in an isolation cell, that he suffered terrible torture because the Serbs had learned that his brother was with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know what happened to him and how he fared. All I know is that he spent a long time in an isolation cell and that he was beaten several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From people who talked to him, who communicated with him. He was released from the isolation cell later on and was with us, but we could often see how they would take him out through the gate, and on his way back, and he always looked terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he looked terrible, could you be a little bit more specific? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a beaten-up man. I mean, how can he look but terrible? He could barely move. There were visible injuries as a consequence of torture, of mistreatment. Why, I don't know, but he had terrible difficulty walking, so both his feet or legs must have been injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on Schedule C, number 28 is Munib Veiz. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him too. He was a salesman before the war. I think he was killed in that room, the same night that Nurko Nisic was killed, and those others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also interrogated several times and beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him also with injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was in the adjoining room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you believe that he was killed the same night as Nurko Nisic? Did you see him or learn that he was taken out that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other people saw it - I did not - how he had been -- that he was taken out that night; people who were in the same room with him in the old wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll now go through Schedules A and B. Again I'll follow the same format and read out specific names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Schedule A, number 4, is the name of Halim Corovic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not really sure if that's the person I have in mind. The village of Kamen. I'm not -- Room 18, perhaps he was with me. I think he is the third person that I found in that isolation cell with two doors during the interrogation when I saw Aziz Sahovic and Rizvanovic. I think he was the one, but I did not know him personally, yet I think it was that Corovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A-6 is Halim Dedovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him personally, a hairdresser. He was taken on the 11th or the 12th of December with a group of six other men. No trace of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the six other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fahrudin Malkic; Aziz Sahovic; Ekrem Cengic; and Ibro Karovic, Ibro, Ibrahim Karovic. This last one -- at least, that was the story. I don't know, because I did not communicate with him, but I heard from other people that he was a journalist who had been captured somewhere on the front line and accused of spying. One of the prisoners mentioned even his name, said he was Alojz or something like that. They were called out in the evening from the rooms, then taken to a separate room, and the next morning I saw them in front of the entrance into the KP Dom, into the camp, and they stood there for a while and then they were taken out, and all trace has been lost of them ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "all trace has been lost of them," did you -- do you know what efforts were made to locate them? Do you know if their family members communicated with you that they were looking for these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. People are trying to find out something to this day. Malkic's brother and a friend of mine and my relative was married to him. He did his utmost. He tried all -- even through Vojislav Maksimovic, because they used to be friends, he tried to find out the truth about them through him, but nobody ever found out the truth. All that we know is that they are missing. And relatives of other people were trying to trace them, and are still trying to trace them, and they asked me questions too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit more specific and tell us which relatives were asking you about their loved ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said about Malkic, then Sahinovics, Dedovics, those largely, but I knew about others too, because people are feverishly trying to find out all those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say no trace was heard of particular individuals, is that what you mean, that their relatives approached you for information about what happened to their loved ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are trying everything to find out. We are trying to do it, and others, and with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Schedule B, number 2, is Nedzib Babalija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in Room 18 with me. He was brought shortly after I came to the camp, and he arrived with a rather large group from Miljevina. I believe he worked in the mine before the war. He was a mining technician and he was brought -- when he was brought, we could see that he had been beaten. His eye was almost closed; it was all black and blue. And he was also beaten all over his body. And for a long time his eye was all bloody. And he was taken away. There is no trace of him. I don't know exactly when he was taken away. And his relatives also tried to find out something about him from me, and I communicated with them in Herzegovina, with his parents and his sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he ever beaten during interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the camp, yes. He was already beaten when he arrived there, and then he was taken for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he was taken for interrogation at the KP Dom, do you know if he was beaten further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told me so. Very few people went through those interrogations without beatings, very few, and I was one of those. And some people never went to make any statements at all, and others gave I don't know how many statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Schedule B, number 11, is Zaim Cedic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know several Cedics, but I'm not sure about their first names. There were Cedics in Cohodar Mahala who were in the camp and who are missing. And there were also Cedics above Brod at Trnovace and Trbusce, and they had never been brought, and their relatives had been told that they were in the camp, because local Serbs, local villagers, told them so. But from that area, from Trnovace, Trbusce, Kosman, Popov Most, very few people from there, from those places, were brought to the KP Dom. As a matter of fact, the majority of them were never taken to the KP Dom, we never saw them there, and they include a large number of my relatives also from Kosman. Because later on, through communication, through contacts, we heard that they had been caught and captured and arrested and taken for interrogation to KP Dom, but we never saw them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those relatives of yours, were they ever heard from again, the ones who were allegedly brought to the KP Dom but whom you never saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were Cedics from Cohodar Mahala who were brought to the KP Dom. Could you tell us their names, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Schedule B, number 12, is Murat Crneta.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him personally before the war. A short man, dark-haired, an engineer, worked at Maglic. He was also taken to pick plums. And as we have already said, I believe his body was identified, that it was found in a mass grave in a stream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-24 is Resad Hadzimesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Resad Hadzimesic and his brother - I think his name is Mirsad - two brothers from Aladza, they were brought to the camp. They were also taken to pick plums. I was not present. I told you because I went out to work - that is, I left early in the morning and returned in the afternoon - so that I could not really see with my own eyes how each one of those groups were taken out. But later on, when talking to those people and then through contacts with their relatives or specifically with his wife in Mostar, he -- she had been told that he had gone to pick plums. She was told that by other people who had seen that. And he is missing now. But two people saw him. He was a driver in the KP Dom -- sorry, no, not in the KP Dom, in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you go on, when was he seen in the health centre? After he'd gone to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's a good question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is impossible, Your Honour. Before the war, he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was a driver. He was a driver in the health centre. My wife worked there too. Yesterday, we forgot about one thing. I don't know whether I should say that today or shall we come back to it later on. When you asked me if I had -- when I heard the order to go to work again, whether I did do that. I did. And so did my wife and my uncle, because they are health workers and they reported to the health centre. But they -- when they got there, for two hours nobody said a word to them, and then a doctor approached them and whispered to them, "Just get lost." So that they were also removed from their jobs. And Hadzimesic was brought to the KP Dom, and after that, he did not go back to the health centre to work as a driver. That I'm sure about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Hadzimesic was brought from the health centre to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know that, where he was brought from. It's quite possible but I just don't know that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I still think we need to have an express statement that he was seen at the health centre before he was taken to the KP Dom, because the statement that he made - and it's open to two interpretations - was, "He was seen in the KP Dom -- sorry, no, not in the KP Dom, in the health centre." Now if you could just ask him precisely when it was he was last seen in the health centre, it will clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us first of all when Mr. Hadzimesic was last seen in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was around the 10th or the 12th of April. My wife and my uncle went to work in the health centre and it was then that they saw him. What happened afterwards, we lost all contact with him because he lived in a different part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was brought to the KP Dom, you saw him at the KP Dom, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought to the KP Dom before me. I was brought there on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last time, when was the last time that people saw him at the KP Dom? Was that when he was taken out to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- did you ever hear of anybody seeing him after that, after he was taken out to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said earlier that there were efforts by his family, I think it was his wife, to locate him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His wife lived in Mostar then. When I came out of the camp, I visited Mostar once and I spoke with her and she asked me about it and then his sister also did all within her power to find that out. She lived in Zagreb at the time. But there is no trace. Neither of them found any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Move on now to Schedule B, number 30, Kemo Isanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kemo Isanovic from Cohodar Mahala, a young guy. He was taken away. I saw how they took him away with Mersud Pasovic at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was that? How was he taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I saw was how they took them outside the KP Dom, beat them and shoved them onto a truck -- onto a van, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-30 -- sorry, did you ever see him again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-31 is Ibro Kafedzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Ibro Kafedzic. I think I -- a while ago I gave you a wrong name of those five or six people. He was taken away. Kafedzic, Karovic; I may have confused those two when I said that they were taken on the 10th or the 12th of December. It was this one who was taken away, Ibro Kafedzic. He was in room 18 with me and he was brought at about the same time, and with visible injuries as a result of beatings. And he was taken for interrogation several times at the same time when I was taken for interrogations too. And he told me that they beat him terribly because a relative of his - and he said he hardly knew the man - that that relative had joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that was the only reason why they beat him so badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, earlier you gave us the name of Ibro Karovic and you're correcting it now to Ibro Kafedzic. It's not Karovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it, yes, yes. He was the one who was taken away with the group that included Markic, Sahinovic, Ekrem Cengic and Fehim Dedovic. No, Halim Dedovic, I apologise. Fehim Dedovic is a different man, who came out of the camp but then died immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Schedule B, number 32 is Rasim Kajgana, and you've already told us that he was taken out as one of the plum pickers and someone saw his body. Did you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it might be interesting to tell you that he was brought with a group of people from Montenegro. On the eve of the war, they had sought sanctuary there, who were evidently clever enough and thought -- and decided to escape, knew what would happen and they escaped. But some people then went to those refugee camps and simply rounded up those people, and one night, they brought a bus full of those people to the KP Dom. It was dark already and all those people were put up in a room above me and that group included quite a number of people from Foca and I knew quite a number of them; Kajgana, Sefko Kubat, who died in the camp, Nedzib Lojo and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did Mr. Kubat die in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a very sick man. He had a very bad ulcer, a stomach ulcer or -- I don't know exactly, but he was very sick. He said once that he had to go to hospital to have surgery, but it was necessary to donate blood for that. A few people volunteered, including myself. He was returned from hospital, I don't know exactly, four, five, seven days later. He was returned to the room. He was a bit better at first but then his condition deteriorated. Soon after that, he died. Later on, I heard from some of the hospital staff that he could not be saved, that he was very ill, apparently that he had some kind of a tumor, but it is inconceivable since they knew anyway, I mean the staff at the KP Dom, since they knew what kind of a serious patient this was, that he could live only for about a month or whatever, why didn't they let him die a free man among his own people and have a dignified funeral? They knew it. He died at the KP Dom and that's where he was buried as well. That is to say, at a locality elsewhere, a cemetery downstream from town, that is to the north of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you learned from the hospital staff that he could not be saved. How did you learn from the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It so happened that a few times I met people who worked there, but that was much later. I told you that I knew all those people well because my wife had worked there for many years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this the hospital staff at the Foca hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned also that a group of people were brought from Montenegro, that they were rounded up. Do you know who rounded up those people; what authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs from Foca came, Stefanovic -- oh, what was his first name? He went to school with me. Miodrag? I'm not sure about his name, Stefanovic at any rate. He had a privately owned restaurant and he introduced himself as an inspector and then, with the assistance of the local authorities, he obtained information as to where these people were accommodated because they had to register with the police because of their temporary residence there. And others were put up at various resorts, whatever. Some -- and then they picked them up and some were even in prison, in the local prisons there, and then they were all rounded together and brought to Foca to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this what the people brought from Montenegro told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We talked. Afterwards, when we would meet and when some of them came to my room, Sefko Kubat told me about it, Rasim Kajgana did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Schedule B, number 37 is Emir Mandzo, could you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a young man. He's related to my wife. He lived near the hospital, in an area called Mijakovic, I guess. I think that's the other Mandzo who was supposed to be interrogated instead of Salko Mandzo, Kelta. I don't know whether we got this right yesterday. He's been missing too. There has been no trace of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he is related to your wife. Has your wife or any other members --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- heard from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never; no one, no one ever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, I swear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-40 is Avdo Mehmedspahic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him too from before the war. We were schoolmates. He worked at Velefarmacija. I know that after he was brought to the camp, he spent a long time at the isolation cell. He was beaten terribly. I don't know what happened to him afterwards. Perhaps he was transferred from the isolation cell to some room. I don't know, because when we were taken out for lunch, only the people from one room would be taken out for lunch or for dinner, so we didn't really meet during 1992, and for a long part of 1993 as well. And I also went out to work. I went out in the morning and I came back in the evening. I didn't see him in the room afterwards, but I know for sure that he had been at the isolation cell and that a few times he was taken out from the isolation cell for interrogations. One Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. man told me that they had beaten him terribly on the soles of his feet and that he could hardly move, that he had terrible haematoma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man told you that Mr. Mehmedspahic was beaten on his feet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was beaten in the isolation cell or in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about anybody being beaten at the isolation cell. Usually they take people out, either into the area just before one entered the isolation cells - that is also where they beat me when they were taking me out of the isolation cell after my attempted escape - or they were taken to the gate, and then they were beaten over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number B-41 is Asim Mezbur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asim Mezbur, yes. Yes, correct. Photographer. I knew him for many years before the war. He's a disabled person. He didn't have a hand and a big part of his arm. He was brought from his home, together with his brother, Esad. As I said yesterday, during the first months of 1992, in the camp in 1992, that is, the staff of the KP Dom and Rasevic and Todovic would often enter the compound and go over there to the restaurant. Among them there were also some officers, soldiers. I don't know who all. Once Asim called out to a man whom he knew. He was wearing a uniform and he had a little bag. He was saying hello to him from the window. He was sort of asking him to help him. But this man said, "We found a transmitter at your place, a radio transmitter." And you know what they found? They found not a mobile phone, not a cell phone, but a cordless phone. Because then, at home, he did not have a telephone line. He had not had a telephone line before that. And then in Germany he bought this cordless phone with a long range, and the telephone was actually installed in his photography shop and he needed it because of his work. So he would carry this cordless phone with him, the mobile part of the cordless phone, you see. And this friend of his knew that that was a telephone, that it was not a radio transmitter, you see, but they needed to have a reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Mezbur as a result of this accusation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's been no sign of him. He's been taken away and there has been no trace of him since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B-52 is Mesa Sofradzija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can we go back to this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I told you just now was something that Asim Mezbur told me about personally. He told me what they were charging him with and that that is why he had terrible problems. As for Mr. Sofradzija, I knew him personally as well before the war. He worked at the municipality as a clerk in the water management sector. He was arrested in Novi Sad, where he had sought shelter before the war with the intention of - how should I put this? - of escaping this hell. However, his brother was an officer. I think he was a Major in the Yugoslav army. But somehow they found out - I don't know how - that he was there. They came, they picked him up and brought him to the KP Dom. He personally told me about this once when we saw each other in passing, when I was being taken out to work. This was while we were still coming from different rooms. And in the morning I was going to work, and his room, the people from his room, were returning from breakfast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sofradzija suffer consequences because of his brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't confirm that with 100-per-cent certainty. I just know that he was taken out for interrogations, that he was beaten up. I did not talk to him after that. This first conversation was just after he was brought into camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at the KP Dom with injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also taken in this period of August/September, one of those groups. As I said, I worked outside almost every day. I did not see. I could not personally see when people's names were being called out and when these people were taken to the gate, you know. However, he has disappeared. There's been no trace of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "August and September," that was 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now from the schedules and ask you some questions about the land mines, both in KP Dom and outside. Do you know if there were land mines inside the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. The entire area inside was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And of course Mr. Warden knows about it too, and he can confirm that. Well, I know. I saw the people who did that. One of them, who was sort of their leader, he told me about it later. And I asked him, "What were you doing?" and he said, "We were laying mines," as if it was requested from the KP Dom to have this area mined, that is, within the walls, within the walls that surround the KP Dom. Later, when I worked at the furniture factory, I could see the mines quite clearly, those that were placed, and a few times they were activated. Once, this was - I don't know - it was either a cat or a dog, and once it was a Serb soldier, a Montenegrin volunteer, Djapic, who worked with us from time to time at the furniture factory. They had well-established channels for getting alcohol from the other side of the camp where the forest and the hill was, and he was boasting and saying that he knew so well how the mines were placed that he could dance between and among them. However, one day he did step on a mine. His leg was blown up, and they brought him to the exit of the KP Dom on some kind of a small cart that was used for transportation within the furniture factory. One of them, a friend of his, looked at our rooms and hollered at us, said, "This is because of you balijas," as if his friend Djapic had been killed on account of us, because these mines had been laid on account of us, you see. As I said yesterday, the bars in Room 13 were allegedly put because of us. In the previous prison, when convicts were there, convicts who were convicted for various crimes they had committed, they didn't have any bars there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify a few things: When you said the Serb soldier or the volunteer from Montenegro was inside the KP Dom and got blown up or got injured by the mine, what was he doing inside the KP Dom? Why was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the details, why who was locked up. I mean, look: They would get drunk at the front line, they would fight amongst themselves. That was usually on account of looting, whatever. There were various other conflicts. People were locked up for three, five, ten days, or even longer than that. Although perhaps it may be of interest if I say that many local Serbs went through the KP Dom because they didn't want to join the army, the Serb army. I personally know them. They tried in every way. Some fled, and others tried to get off the hook in different ways. They asked doctors for certificates stating that they were incapacitated, that they could not go, et cetera. Djapic, specifically, he was a volunteer from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people that you described, these different groups of people, those who had been involved in fights or people who were trying to avoid military service, those were Serbs that were imprisoned in KP Dom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right. Yes. They were imprisoned, but they were separated from us, and it was strictly forbidden to have any kind of contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Djapic, if he was imprisoned at KP Dom, how was it that he was able to walk outside where there were land mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was detained at the KP Dom, but he was one of the free men, so to speak. He was free to leave his room, as opposed to us, and he worked at the furniture factory. That's where he went to work. And that happened beyond the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, were the Serb prisoners allowed to move around outside their rooms even when they weren't working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Their rooms were open. They could go out whenever they wanted to. They could visit with one another, they could go out into the compound, into the yard, they could walk about, they could receive visitors; everything, everything which was unimaginable for us. Only during the later months, half-hour walks were allowed for inmates who did not go to work. But whether we could go out and walk and receive visits and things like that, that was unimaginable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "later months," what time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could not tell you exactly now, the exact time, the exact period when it was allowed, when the inmates were allowed to do that. None of us were convicts. We were never convicted of anything. We never got any paper stating that we were charged with such-and-such a crime that we had committed or that we were convicted. I don't know how many months had passed by. Perhaps it was the end of 1992 or beginning of 1993. Once a day, people were allowed to go out for a short walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to have you shown Exhibit P6 again, with the assistance of the usher, so you can show us exactly where the land mines inside the KP Dom were located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is the way it was: This is the entrance from the street for freight vehicles, trucks. This is a wall, the wall of the camp. Mines were placed within the walls, here, all the way up to the top, then Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. along this wall, and then down here, all the way down here. There was a gate here on the wall, and that's where the road was, where materials were brought for the furniture factory; that is to say, wooden boards, wood in general, et cetera. So let me repeat: This entire area, all the way up to the top here, to the north, and down here, to the new wing of the administration building, to the very entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to summarise or describe what you've indicated to us. You said that there was -- you started at the point where there is a vehicle entrance to the KP Dom, which would be in the lower right-hand corner of Exhibit P6, and you indicated that the wall of the KP Dom starts at the far right edge, is a line that goes straight up and then turns left. Inside, just directly inside that wall that is on the diagram, to the left, and then as you run up the top to the bottom of that wall, all along that perimeter were the land mines. Then about halfway through this diagram, the wall runs down. And again that wall -- along that wall are the mines. And you stopped at the point where the wall meets what you've referred to as the new part of the administration building. And the gate that you indicated as going to the furniture factory is about a third of the way down from that wall that's on the left-hand side. So all along the inside perimeter of the right-hand side, top side and left-hand side of the wall to the KP Dom is where you've indicated that there were land mines. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely right. There were mines all along the walls on the inside except here where the road is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where the road is is the road into the furniture factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, correct. It goes by the heating room, by the metal shop, to the furniture factory. This here is the storage area. This is a big terrace, actually, that has no walls. It just has pillars and a roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that located? You went a little bit too fast for me to follow that. The place where you said had no roof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness has indicated now a rectangle which is to the left of what has been marked as the furniture factory but still within the compound of the KP Dom. And just for the record, the road that the witness referred to, he started to describe how it went from the metal factory, and that would be from -- it appears to be an exit to the left-hand side of the furniture -- I'm sorry, of the metal workshop, the metal workshop, going up and to the right, outside the KP Dom, and then re-entering the KP Dom at the gate that goes toward the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, do you know where Mr. Djapic was injured by the land mine? Can you locate that for us or do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. It was in this part here, this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness is indicating the area between the furniture factory and the top -- the wall on the top part of the exhibit, about halfway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean the perimeter fence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The perimeter fence, yes. And that would be behind -- or on this diagram, on top of the furniture factory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, you started to tell us how you knew that the land mines were being put in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may be an appropriate time, seeing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- it's almost 11.00. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, before the break, you told us that you saw the land mines being laid at KP Dom. Could you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the summer of 1992, shortly after I arrived in the camp. Not right away but perhaps a month later. I know the man who did that, who put the mines. Some years before that we used to work together for the auto service at Brod, near Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him laying the mines, was he wearing a uniform? Do you know in what capacity he was laying the mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met in passing. We were going for -- out for breakfast and we came across each other in the yard of the KP Dom. We had gone in for breakfast and he was walking towards the gate and we stood there for a moment. We met in the doorway, so I said, "Bozo Saja" - Bozo Saja is his name - "What are you doing here?" And he said, "Well, we have come to put the mines because those from the administration had requested us to do it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say why the administration had requested it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't go into any details, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it is quite obvious why it was done and because of whom it was done. It was obviously done because of us, because they must have assumed that we'd try to escape. Perhaps they thought we'd attempt a collective escape or a subversion or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever warned about the land mines? In other words, did people from the prison staff say, "Don't try to escape because there are land mines here"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to me directly, nobody, but when I worked in the furniture factory, a couple of people drew our attention to it, as we worked there, to take care not to come close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person that you mentioned, who told you he was there to lay mines, did he give you -- did he specify what administration he was referring to? Did he mean or did he say the administration of the KP Dom or did he specify what he meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, administration is one thing and command is another thing. The leadership of the camp was the administration; that is how we referred to them, not the command. And the -- and vice versa. So it is quite obvious that it was the camp administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about mines that were not inside the KP Dom. Did you know if any detainees were ever taken to clear mines, say at the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It happened, yes. I know that. I'm positive. A driver from my room went with a car, with a freight car, in front of them, Saban Karup, and it happened once, he told me about it later on, that he'd passed with his car, and the car which was behind him came upon a mine, and on that occasion, some Serbs wanted to kill him. Another said, "Well, listen, it was God's will for him to pass through and survive," so that he survived. And I also know another case of Muhamed Ahmetkadic in the metal shop, in the car shop. We had put back together a large freight truck, a cistern, as we call them. It was a closed van, closed truck, which was used to transport furniture. And he took it to go towards Gorazde. Three or four days later, that Ahmetkadic returned and was kept in the isolation room for a long time. He never came out. In the new wing of the building, on the upper floor. And I came across him when I left the isolation cell about a month later, and he told me that he was driving towards Gorazde, planning to demine that road, to try to pass through and deactivate the mines so that the Serb army could enter Gorazde, but when they got up there, they realised it was impossible, that he could not get through the whole mine field, and so they turned him back. And I also know, during my stay in the isolation cell, a guy who was in the isolation cell 4 until the end, Omer Bavcic from Gorazde who was captured somewhere on the demarcation line. He was taken a couple of times to go through mine fields, and Serb soldiers then put in his ears those metal rings of the mines, of grenades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the meaning of that, to put those in his ears?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, could also be but simply to vent their anger or whatever on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it meant to humiliate him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All three of these individuals that you mentioned -- Mr. Karup, Mr. Ahmetkadic and Mr. Bavcic - were they detainees at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karup, Ahmetkadic, and Bavcic, Omer. Yes. Yes, correct. Yes, they were. Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who took them to clear the mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you who that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to clarify and just to make the record clear, were they told to drive ahead of Serb army vehicles so that if there were a land mine, they would get injured or killed rather than the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Karup is listed in Schedule E at number 33. And Mr. Ahmetkadic, there is a Mustafa listed at Schedule E, number 2, although the witness has said his first name is Muhamed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Ahmetkadic was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Yes, quite right. Muhamed. I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when Mr. Ahmetkadic was brought back from driving the vehicle ahead of the military, the Serb military, that he was placed in an isolation cell. Do you know why that was done? Was there a pattern of people being placed in isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. I don't think it is solitary confinement; I think it is an isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's what I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question is: "Was there a pattern of people being placed in isolation cells?" It may be that your translation was different, but in each -- Ms. Kuo has said it twice, "... that he was placed in an isolation cell. Do you know why that was done? Was there a pattern of people being placed in isolation cells?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is quite right. I understood the question was about the isolation cell, but the witness spoke about isolation, not about solitary confinement, and a room for isolation is not the same thing as a solitary confinement room. That is the difference, if my learned friend will agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How far back did the witness refer to this? I wasn't conscious of him saying anything other than "isolation." Yes, here it is. It's at page 35, line 18: "And I also know, during my stay in the isolation cell, a guy who was in the isolation cell." So, as I say, Mr. Bakrac, it may be the translation had a different spin on it, but in each case we have received the word "isolation." You proceed, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you looked like you were about to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Rather, Muhamed Ahmetkadic was taken out of the collective room where we were together. After he returned, he was put in the isolation room. He had no contact with anyone. But that was not the solitary confinement room on the ground floor. And the same thing happened to Karup. And Omer Bavcic was taken out of the solitary confinement room, where I spent a month, and then he was taken back to the solitary confinement room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the witness to clarify for us where these rooms are located so that there's no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "isolation cell," could you tell us what building and what floor you mean? Not the solitary confinement, but the isolation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the new room of the building, on the topmost floor, I don't know whether it's Room 23 or 25, but I know the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "the new building," you mean the prisoners' quarters, not the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They both have them, both the old and the new.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit P6/5, and that should show the top floor of the prisoners' quarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this part of the building, the new part of the building, on the topmost floor, on this side. Now, whether it was Room 23 or 25, I'm not sure about the number, but that was a room in the attic. That was the topmost storey, and that is where Muhamed was kept and where Saban was kept. And after they came out of solitary confinement, 28 days later, I saw Ahmetkadic in Room 18, in this part of the dormitory. And in this part of the dormitory there were five Croats. This was another isolation room. They did not go out to the restaurant for meals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: All right. For the record, the witness first showed what's been marked on this exhibit as Room 23, and then when he referred to Room 28 - I'm sorry - room 18, he moved over the diagram on this picture to where it's marked 22, but he said on a different floor, and I don't think there's a dispute that Room 18 is located there but on a lower floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness? You wanted to say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you do so, I don't think any of us on the Bench are getting the video evidence. I picked up what was actually being shown on the public area, but we're not getting it at the moment on the other channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Perhaps we can move away from the diagram for now and we can come back to it when the problem has been fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, you've said a couple of things and I'd like to ask you to clarify them. You showed Room 23 and you said that that was used as an isolation cell. Were there not regular prisoners kept in that room, or was it used strictly to keep people in a form of isolation, as you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only so as to isolate. Muhamed Ahmetkadic was alone, was completely alone, as I have said. When I came out of the solitary confinement and came to Room 18, I found him and five Croats there, and that was on the same day as the second visit of the Red Cross to the camp in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to being brought to Room 18 and finding the five Croats there, was that after your attempted escape, when you were brought back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in solitary confinement -- those Croats were brought while I was in solitary confinement from somewhere on -- from some part of the front in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to get a clear picture for the Court. That was in July of 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, listen. I escaped on the 8th of July, and I spent two days in the solitary confinement at the gate. And then I spent 27 or 28 days in this solitary confinement cell in the new wing of the building. And then I came out and went to Room 18, and it was then that I found those Croats. So it could have been August; August, yes, not July. Well, they may have been brought in July, but I did not see them then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw them in August of 1993 in Room 18, was Room 18 being used to house the workers' group any more or was it just the five Croats there and then you were brought and then Mr. Ahmetkadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the room for workers. It was the isolation room. The work group was in the old wing, in the building's old wing. As I told you, and I'll repeat it, this was the isolation room with Ahmetkadic and those five Croats who were very quickly taken away, or rather, were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again just talking about Room 18, you had been in Room 18 in the summer of 1992. In the summer of 1993, Room 18 was serving a different function; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes. It is right. Because we have to remember that we were frequently moved from one room to another, that in the summer of 1992, there were very few of us there because people had been taken for exchanges, for so-called exchanges before that. Some of them did come through but most of them, unfortunately, did not. So that people from different rooms were put together, concentrated in smaller areas. In the summer of 1993, we were in the old wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there has been some discussion about the difference between solitary confinement and isolation cell. We understand that there are specially designed solitary confinement rooms, and the rooms that you've pointed out to us, 23 and 18, were not those specially designed solitary confinement rooms, right? I mean, they were regular prisoners' quarters that were being used for a specific purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just common prisoners' quarters, which were -- except that they were used to isolate. And solitary confinement cells were on the ground floor in the new wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking about Mr. Ahmetkadic, do you know why he was isolated after being taken to clear mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. He told me. So as not to tell other inmates where he'd been, why he'd been there, whom he had seen there. They -- I mean the authorities really paid great -- accorded great importance to it, to -- not to allow us get any information from outside, from the outside world. They really tried hard to keep them down to the minimum. They were absolutely -- they were panic-stricken that we might learn about anything from outside. So any radio, television, any communication with the outside world was -- anything like that was prohibited. They wanted to keep a complete media -- to impose a complete media blockade on us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to Mr. Ahmetkadic, did you know of other people who were isolated in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I already said Saban Karup was isolated for a while. I don't know about others in relation to this case, those people who went to clear the mines and tried to break -- to make -- to pave -- to make a passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the authorities were trying to prevent any communication between the detainees and the outside world. Did you have a form of communication with the outside world? For instance, through a radio or other means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shortly after the establishment of the camp, people had TV sets in the rooms, which had stayed from before. That is the prewar prison. And in many lockers that belonged to former convicts, they found transistor radios, but all those transistors were seized in the early months of the camp existence. TV sets were taken away immediately, after a few days only. I did not find any of those things when I arrived on the 20th of May. And the last radio that we had, that was a small transistor, was brought by people from Room 13. A person who is listed under 210 and Uzeir Hadzalic, when the work group was set up, they brought that transistor with them. However, we could use it only for a very short time. We listened to it, hoping we'd get information about whether peace would be signed and would there be an international intervention, would the International Red Cross come, would there be any exchanges. We really wanted to know about this badly. But one of the inmates, in a desperate attempt to come by a piece of bread or a cigarette, he, as we put it, snitched on us. That is, he told -- he talked to a guard and the award was a slice of bread and a cigarette. And after that, the guards began to call out all of us in the room, one by one, and finally, called out me, and the person on 210. Of course, they knew, and those before us had already confirmed, that we indeed had a transistor so it would have served no purpose to say that we didn't. We turned over the transistor and I was put in solitary confinement that day and I was beaten on the back, and that was it that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milutinovic - I don't know his first name - was the one who beat me. I think he comes from Govsa, from Jelec, from somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He beat me with a baton, on my back, on my arms. A couple of blows were in the head and one of them was terribly painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if other people were beaten because of the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know several of them were beaten. I don't know how many because I was taken to a separate solitary confinement cell in the upper part of the row of solitary confinement cells. And other people were beaten in the hallway and in the lower row of the solitary confinement cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then hear that they were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I could. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about an incident in late August or September, 1992, when you were taken out toward the river bank on the River Drina, in front of the KP Dom. Did you on that occasion see any dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the water on the right bank of the Drina, that is on the bank nearer the KP Dom, I saw several bodies there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, what were you doing in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and the individual 210 went to the pile of -- to a heap of rubble which had been brought from the site where Aladza mosque had stood and had been mined.
