And the personnel of the metal shop had ordered us to go and get the copper plate because the Aladza mosque had been covered with copper plate, and they wanted this plate and they wanted to take it to Montenegro and sell it there as refuse and thus pocket some money. And we worked there on the river bank and getting the -- what was left of this brass, of this copper plate. I saw some bodies, or rather, I heard first a guard say to people who were working above us, building a new bunker, a new fortification, and that is a small metal kiosk, a small guard booth, and they were surrounding it with sand, with bags with sand, and I heard a guard called Burilo, nicknamed Busi, how he says -- how he said, "Well, push this shit downstream. Let them flow to Gorazde." Then I raised my head and I saw those bodies. There was a lot of garbage there on the bank. It is quite possible that there was a number of bodies there, at least three or more, but I'm quite positive that I saw two bodies. I saw two bodies. The water is very shallow there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the bodies? Were they male or female and what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 100 per cent sure that these were men wearing civilian clothes. I could not see anything else precisely, not even their age or injuries they might have had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they actually in the water? Did they appear to have come ashore from the water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were in the water. They were not ashore. I repeat, the water was shallow there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the water always shallow there or does it depend on the time of year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the summer of 1992, September. I don't know the exact date, but in that period, the water level is very, very low.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you said were building or putting the sand bags around the kiosk to build a bunker, were they detainees from the KP Dom as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Only inmates worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do when Burilo said to push the bodies into the water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I could not see that because this guard came and we were supposed to transfer these pieces to the metal shop. But I think they pushed them. Because you could not refuse to carry out orders, especially not of that Burilo. That was inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Usher, I'd like to have the witness shown again Exhibit P6. I would ask him to show us on the diagram where this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the computer is working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here, this part, just opposite the gate leading into the KP Dom. In this part, there is an asphalt area where there is a big parking lot. And in this part, there is a parking lot for old vehicles, used vehicles. We worked here. I and the person who is mentioned as 210, we worked here on the shore. The other inmates were working about 20, 25 metres away from me, upstream, and they were fortifying the bunker that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the record, the witness has shown as the big asphalt area a place -- the middle to the bottom of Exhibit P6, there is a big, looks like an empty area, and it's to the left of the bridge and to the right and above what's been marked as the River Drina. And just again to indicate the place where the witness said he was working with 210 is directly above where the word "Drina" appears, and then the place where he said the other detainees were working is slightly to the right of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The River Drina flows in which direction, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness is indicating a direction from right to left and, in fact, that's the arrow that's also drawn to the left of the word "Drina," showing the flow of the water. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before I get to your escape attempt, I had a question about something you had said earlier. You stated yesterday that there were times when you saw the light on in the warden's office in the evening. And in your testimony today, at one point, you said that in the early months of your detention, there were no lights in the evening. Could you clarify that? When you said today that there were no lights in the evening, what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some days when there wasn't any power at all. For a long time, our rooms didn't have any, even when they did, when the administration did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the first few months that you were in KP Dom, the administration building did have electricity and light sources even in the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. I think that the witness said that often there were no lights, either in the prisoners' quarters or in the administration building, and when they did have some, that it would happen that the prisoners' quarters did not have any but that the administration building did. And my friend paraphrased -- she actually phrased her question this way, as if the administration invariably had power and the prison quarters did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I did not intend to create that impression. I did mean to negate the blanket assertion that there was no power at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it's probably equivocal. In the light of the answer, it's a bit difficult to read it that way, but Mr. Bakrac is nothing if not precise about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would be best to do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first few months when you were in KP Dom, there were times when there was light available in the administration building, even when there was no light available to the prisoners' quarters in the evening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also want to ask you a question that I forgot to ask when we were discussing land mines. Do you know if anybody inside the KP Dom was ever killed by a land mine -- by driving over a land mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of one case when driver Drakul got killed, Milivoj Drakul, but that was not within the KP Dom and it's not related to the KP Dom. This was downstream, to the north of the camp, at Josanica. I don't know how come he was going there in the first place in a car, but I just know that he did get killed. There weren't any combat operations there, but I know for sure that there were land mines in many places. They were put there either according to plan or without any plan. Just before I tried to escape, I heard some people saying that below Maglic - that's at Brod, three kilometres away from Foca, upstream - that a fisherman got killed, Skobo - I knew him - because the area around the factory was mined, on the bank of the Drina River. So I was guided by that. When I came to that place, I went to the forest, uphill. I did not go below that factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to Drakul, when he was killed by the land mine, do you know if he was there -- you said he was a driver. Was he there to detect land mines for the Serb military or was he there for other reasons, perhaps personal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know what job he had there, but he did go officially in a car. I mean, whether they needed something personal or whatever, but it's not that he went there to work for the military, to demine it or something like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the person mentioned as Drakul is listed on the employee list, Exhibit P3, at number 90, and there is an indication there that he was killed by a land mine 26th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zekovic. Now we'll move to your attempted escape. Could you tell us why you decided at that particular point to try to escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all awaiting the visit of the Red Cross feverishly, with great anticipation. As I said, it only happened on the 13th of June, 1993. On that occasion, in the room, I and person 210 seized an opportunity to talk to the staff from the International Red Cross on our own. They were two women. I spoke English and my friend spoke French. We asked specifically and directly what our chances were of having them release us, because we were civilians; we were brought from our homes. We were pinning our hopes on the Red Cross, hoping that they would come and see us some day, and that we would explain that we had done nothing and that we were staying there under terrible conditions, and that they would set us free. However, they said to us that this was virtually impossible, absolutely, and that it was still a big question whether they would come again at all and when they would come again. They said that when they would get permission from Pale -- I mean, when they would get permission from Pale, then the Foca people would not let them go into the camp. I personally saw, at least three or four times, vehicles of the International Red Cross in front of the entrance to the KP Dom. So having realised that, I lost every illusion that we would be set free soon. I started thinking about an escape very intensively, straight away. At first I did that together with person 210. However, he vacillated. I don't know. He wasn't brave enough. And then I decided to go for it myself. About six or seven days after that visit of the Red Cross, I had volunteered to go with a group to cut grass and collect it for hay for the farm, because on Saturdays and Sundays, everybody went from the furniture factory and those who did other jobs. There wasn't a strict list. The list was made at the gate itself. However, it so happened that Mitar Rasevic came to the gate and that he asked the guard to call one of the Serbs who had been detained, and he saw me. And he asked me directly, "Zeka, where are you going?" And I said, "Well, I'm going out into the sun as well. I have some problems with my skin, so I'd like to get some sun." And he directly said, "No, you cannot. Go back to your room."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Rasevic told you to go back to your room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that he had his suspicions that I was getting ready to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you done anything to arouse his suspicion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, possibly, in an indirect way. As I worked in the metal workshop doing these different jobs, I had no footwear; I had trainers only. Since a neighbour of mine worked in the administration of the KP Dom, I asked him to bring me a pair of trainers from home, because Vesna, a lady neighbour of ours, the wife of Mate Ivancic, took care of our house. Mate Ivancic was in the camp with me. However, he said that he didn't dare to do that, that he had to talk to someone from the administration. Then once, in passing, I saw Mitar Rasevic and I said that I needed footwear, that I couldn't work in these old ones any longer, that they were falling apart, and he allowed this man to bring me that other pair. A few weeks later, this neighbour did bring these things and they were left in Rasevic's office. Then Rasevic called me and person number 210 and said that we should clean his office, and then he gave me these things. However, Vesna, that lady, that neighbour of mine, she sent all my things: trousers, a shirt, a sweater, a belt, anything but my shoes. The shoes were her husband's, and regrettably they were too small for me. I took all of those things into the camp, into the compound of the KP Dom, because there were some people who didn't have socks, some people who didn't have any underpants, and others who did not have shirts, and I personally did not need that. I only needed shoes. And I assume that Mr. Rasevic based his assumption on that, that I got all these things and that I needed them for the escape, which was not really of crucial importance. As we were let into the compound of the camp after that, I wore some of these things underneath my working clothes and I carried the others, and he said strictly that we should not tell anyone anything about this, that they know everything that is discussed in rooms, and if they find out that he had done that, then they would have terrible problems, he and the man who brought this, and I would probably too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Mr. Rasevic who said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Mitar Rasevic said that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have good relations with Mitar Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not particularly good relations. We knew each other by sight from before the war. But I don't know. He did not treat us at the metal workshop badly. He left a good impression in all these conversations and contacts we had with him. He always said that he felt sorry for us, that he knew that we were innocent and nevertheless detained, and he himself said that it was the creme de la creme that was locked up in there from our town, but he said that he couldn't do anything to help. However, he did not allow it to be called a camp; not only he, but none of the staff, the guards, whoever. They treated it as some kind of protection centre, whatever. And what kind of a protection centre is that? The very fact that the International Red Cross was allowed to visit only in June 1993 speaks for itself. Let me be even more precise. The International Red Cross tried once and they actually got in in April 1992, but that was very short. They entered one room and they managed to make only a partial list of persons' names. But they kicked them out with various threats, saying that, if necessary, they could liquidate them, whatever. I did not see this, I did not experience this, because I came to the camp later, but this is what people who were there said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rasevic say, since he was powerless to do anything, who had the power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not say specifically who did and who didn't, you see, but all of them in individual contacts -- I mean, when I say "all of them," I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say those who we could have contact with. Later, as time went by, there were more and more of them. All of them made an effort to leave the impression that they were good, that they were the good guys, that they had protected us; had it not been for them, we would have been killed or harmed or whatever. And I said, "Why would I be killed? Why would I be harmed when I had never done anything bad to anyone?" And they had no answer to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the time when Mitar Rasevic turned you back from going outside, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came back to the room. Nothing. I felt sorry, because it was an ideal opportunity. They took this vehicle to go to cut grass, all the way to the border with Montenegro, to the village of Hum. It would have been very easy for me to go from there, along the Tara River canyon, which I knew very well, and that I could easily reach Montenegro from there and finally get together with my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you try to escape next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 8th of July, 1993. It was raining hard that morning, and I immediately thought: this is an ideal day for an escape. When I was taken into the compound to go to breakfast, I said to the guard at the gate that I had to go to the room to get some medicines. I went to the room, and underneath my working clothes I put on a jacket similar to the one I'm wearing now. Then I put all of that within the metal workshop. I had a few small things from breakfast, and from the mid-morning snack I had left a slice or two of bread. I had a towel, I had a T-shirt, and - I don't know - I think a pair of socks. And then, in the afternoon, I heard that Relja, the head of the metal workshop, was telling Zuti and Ramiz, the other workers, that he would go to do something at Maglic and that when we finish work at 3.00, that we should leave the keys at the usual place, and he left. I thought that somebody stayed there to guard us, one of the roaming guards, so to speak, from the gate, so I was wondering for a while -- it was hard to make a decision like that because it involved a terrible risk. However, what surfaced then was that great wish that I had to finally get together with my nearest and dearest. I took off my working clothes, I got out of the workshop, I passed by the heating room, I passed by the dogs that were in the lower part of the metal workshop, and I got out into the street. In a guard's hut before that, I saw a raincoat, a cape, sort of. However, I didn't find that. I had seen it before but I didn't find it. And then I just took an ordinary piece of plastic, I put it on my head, and I went out into the road. I was walking upstream. I passed by the entrance to the KP Dom, and then I went right, across the bridge, and then I started going up hill, through meadows and the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there for a moment. Mr. Zekovic, when you passed by the guard booth, was there a guard there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean at the exit where I came out on to the road? No, at that moment, there was no guard there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there normally a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually a guard would be at the guard post. I can show it to you. Below the car shop. And where I came out, at that moment, there were no guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could have the Usher show you Exhibit P6 again, and you can show us where that guard's booth is and the direction that you -- the path that you took.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the metal shop. I came out here, then went by the new wing of the administrative building, by the boiler room, came out above the mechanic shop, and this guard booth is here. This is it. Practically on the road from the town to the hospital. And I went -- I took a road, a path above it, because we often had to go to this area to get some construction materials because that is where those warehouses were. And that exit, I can't really see it here. Oh, yes, it is here. Yes, it's here. Here it is. So I got out on to the road, and I took the road because there was no way I could cross here. And it wasn't all that suspicious because civilians used that road too. It was raining and I had this plastic on my head so that nobody could recognise me. And I walked past the KP Dom and its gate to the bridge here. And then I crossed to the other bank of the Drina towards those villages up in the hills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me briefly describe what you've indicated for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The path that the witness indicated took him from the metal workshop courtyard up through a gap between the metal workshop and the administrative building, going up in the diagram. Then he turned left and went toward where there is a black circle, to the left of where the workshop area was, and that is what he indicated was the guard's hut. And then he went further to the left of the diagram, made a U-turn basically, came back right on the public road, and then continued in the front of the KP Dom across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, that guard's hut that you indicated, which is on this diagram a black circle, once you got past that point, were you out of the KP Dom or were you still within some sort of controlled area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't really give you a definitive answer. There was a guard here, and when we worked, there was a guard here too. Except that it frequently happened -- mind you, it's 1993, that was a long time, and we had been working there for a long time and there were never any incidents. So at times, guards would leave for an hour or two, go to the gate to just talk, socialise and have coffee or perhaps brandy, so that there were times when we would be left alone for long periods of time. But as a rule, there was a guard at this gate here. The guard here, the sentry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were past that point, was that the last guard or the last possible guard that you would encounter before you were in the outside world, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned going past some dogs. Where were the dogs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Above the car repair shop, there were several small buildings where they kept dogs. And then beyond the car repair shop, downstream, and those dogs had long chains and so that they could move around. But we knew those dogs, or rather, they knew us and we often fed them, so that I could walk past them without any problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were these basically guard dogs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zekovic, when you said you headed for the forest, could you tell us where you went from that point on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I planned to go upstream from the camp. It is the left bank of the Drina, to be quite precise, and then at some suitable spot, in some spinney or next to a stream, to wait for the night to fall, because it was dangerous to move about in daytime and I thought I'd wait for the night to fall. I realised that the police would be notified straight away, that there would be a posse, and that is what I did. I waited for the dark. It was cloudy, rain -- there was rain from time to time. I crossed the road, went down to the left bank of the Drina, and I started upstream towards Brod. And I could see on the other side of the Drina fires burning, log fires burning, and it was not logical for them to be fishermen because it was raining and it was just too late for fishermen, and then I was told later on that they had set out patrols to wait for me because they assumed that I would go to the part of the town where I used to live. That is, they assumed that I would go home to my street. But I went upstream instead. Then I swam across the Drina, across the river, and continued upstream and I fetched up near the factory that we said had been mined, where the fishermen, Skobo, had been killed. And then I crossed the road, and when I reached it, before I crossed it, I first spent some time looking out for patrols. And even though there were patrols every 50 metres or so, at a point where I saw that the road was empty, I just ran across the road and I took a dirt road to a village called Subovici or, to be more exact, to the houses who were killed, that is or people who were killed, that is Asim and Esad Mezbur. And that is how far I could get that night because one could not follow the road that I meant to take by night because the forest is very thick there, very dense. And so I waited for the morning there and when the day began to break, I continued through the forest, above an inhabited locality, above a settlement. And when I had already passed that settlement, I had to cross a road which goes from Bunovi to Brod, and I could not cross that road immediately because on the other side -- there was a thicket on the other side, so I had to walk uphill and there I came across two men, first one in civilian clothes, an elderly man, and I said to him -- I asked him, "Did you see some cows? The cows had escaped. We failed to keep them," and did he perhaps -- had he seen them? And was there another village somewhere? And he said that, yes, but it was a long way off. And then I met another man and I repeated this same story about lost cows. And just as I parted company with that second man, I could then turn right and into the forest. And I walked through the forest without difficulty, and I kept my direction. I could see. I could follow the right bank of the river because I told you I was familiar with the ground. And there was no difficulty, no problem at all, until I reached a village called Kopilovi, and the fog from the river had already risen from the river so that I could not see the other side and I was -- I had already climbed down too low when I reached that village. I realised I had to climb up, and I thought that I'd climbed high enough. And from below, from the village, I could hear the sounds of a car. I heard noises -- rather, voices of people, and I assumed it was other army or police. Anyway, their patrol. And from what I remembered, because my mother comes from a neighbouring village, only slightly higher up from that village, and as far as I could remember, the area, I had -- I came out to the meadows where there are no more houses, that is when I finally came out of the fog. I reached those meadows and I thought that I was already past that village, that I was sufficiently high up and all I had to do was to get to an oak forest and then turn towards the village where my -- which was my mother's native village, and up there it was much better because there were not so many settlements, and I intended to move at a higher altitude and therefore go around all those villages. But then I again found myself in the fog. However the wind dispersed it very quickly, and I realised I was in a village, that I was in a village. And 20 metres away from me, two women were picking cherries, and below me, a man with a rifle entered a house. I could see that he was very old. And then I concocted a story for them, and I said, "Where is the road to Kunduci? I need to go see Obren Pejovic to buy a car and I've lost my way, because I came up this road from Bunovi." And they looked at me suspiciously. Evidently, they realised immediately that I was not the one -- that is, I had told them that my name was Zivkovic, and they asked me, "Who are you?" And I went on, trying simply to get out of their sight, and into the woods again. However, it was impossible because on the upper part of the road, the forest was very dense, so that I could only walk straight ahead. And I had covered some 800 to 900 metres and I was right in the thick of the village, that is even more houses, more people. So I told myself there is no way through here, and I went back, thinking I perhaps might try to make my way through this dense forest. But from behind the first curve, a man with a rifle turned up. It was the same man that I had seen with the rifle next to a house. And I tried again to make up a story for him, to explain that I was on my way to Kunduci, looking for Obren Pejovic. And he uncocked his rifle, made a couple of steps back, and said, "Hands up." And then there was no use to try to pretend anything, so that I stopped. And then we walked on, that is in the direction that I had come back from. And there we came to a house and the villagers gathered in no time. There were some troops there and women and old people and children. And they started to discuss what to do with me. Some suggested to take me to Foca and turn me over because they would be rewarded then with at least two canisters of fuel. Others cried out, "Let's tie him up. Let's tie him up." Others again said, "Let's call the patrol." And others again said, "Well, into the brook and cut his throat." And the man next to whose house we were standing said -- or -- and the wife, "Well, the patrol had ordered if we catch him to just keep him and to let them know." And then a young man took my wind jacket off to search the pockets, but I had nothing. I nevertheless had to take it off. And then they brought very thick rope and tied my hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, was it clear to you that the villagers knew who you were, that you had escaped from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely, absolutely. They were notified in all the ways possible. There was Radio Foca and radio communication, whatever, because they knew what I looked like and they gathered the direction in which I had been moving because the person mentioned under number 210 had told them. He tried to apologise to me later on and said, "Zeka, I am sorry, but they had brought a pistol and a rifle and beat you," and he simply told them which direction I would take so that they were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to make sure that the transcript is clear, you said regarding 210, he said, "They brought a pistol and a rifle to beat you." Did you mean that 210 was beaten with the pistol and rifle in order to have him say what your plan was, what direction you would go in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the ethnicity of the villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know it all. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew that it was a Serb village from before. And during that discussion before the police arrived, we talked, and one of them asked me, "Where did you come from? Who is your father?" And I told him the name of my father and he said, "Oh, yes, I know him. Once upon a time he helped me get some tiles for the roof." And another woman said, "Well, where does your mother come from?" And I said, "From over there, from Kunduci." And they said, "Oh, yes, sure. We know them. Nice people, good neighbours." And I said, "Yes, that's quite right. That is all true. But you see what I'm going through? My father was good and all my relatives were good, and look what happened to me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the villagers ever discuss just setting you free?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was tied right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was never -- nobody among the villagers said, "Why don't we just let him go"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a single one. About 40 minutes or so -- I don't know exactly, because I was so scared and so exhausted, you know, that I couldn't really say anything about time, but the civilian police arrived, three guys, and one of them said, "Untie him." And I looked at him and I recognised that policeman, because I used to know him before the war, Milic. We called him Brko. He had a moustache. And then they untied me. And I was all wet; I was soaking wet because I was going through the forest and it rained. And I was sitting under that tree and it was cold and I was shaking. And he said to me, "Go lean against that tree stump and get rest." And at that moment I remember that I had the wind jacket, because I knew they would take me back to the camp and I also knew what was in store for me when I got back to the camp, so it was useful to have a shirt rather than the wind jacket. And I said, "Listen, you know that that bloke took the wind jacket because he wanted to search it," and that young man said, "Keep it. He doesn't need it any more." But Milic nevertheless persisted and got back the wind jacket from him, and I put it on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did you think this wind jacket would be helpful? You said you knew what was coming to you. What were you thinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew. I never had any doubts that it was beating, beating was there for me when I got there, and it would be some help. I mean, I had my shirt and I also had this jacket. Well, it didn't help much, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the civilian police do to you? Did they take you someplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They picked up their Motorola and let know somebody in Foca - I don't know whether it was the police station or whom - to send a car to take me, because we had to come down from the village down to the road, and that is what we did. We climbed down and the car had already arrived. It was a car -- one of the cars of the KP Dom, the so-called Black Maria, you know, the type of van that are used to transport prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it KP Dom staff that brought you back to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were two officers in that van from the KP Dom, Matovic and Miro Prodanovic. Miro Prodanovic asked me straight away, or rather, he abused me verbally and said, "Oh, so you're off to buy some cows." And Matovic did not say anything, but hit me with his fist in the head, and I fell down. The civilian police reacted and said, "You don't have to use force." I did not resist during the arrest. And then they locked me in the Black Maria. We arrived in the town. The civilian police got off and went into the police station and we went to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person Matovic who hit you, do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. Perhaps if I saw a list, perhaps I would have able to identify. There is a Zoran Matovic, but that is not the one. Everybody called him Mata. That was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Matovic listed as a guard who is not Zoran Matovic is Miladin Matovic, on Exhibit P3, number 47. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First name --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at KP Dom, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Miladin. I think you misread it, but Miladin, yes, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They opened the door, I got off, and on the bench next to the door into the KP Dom was Burilo, called Busi. He put down his automatic on the bench, spit out the cigarette that he had -- that he was smoking, and grabbed me, right there, at the entrance, and proceeded to beat me. I tried to defend myself, I tried to dodge, but you must realise he must have weighed at least 100 kilogrammes, if not 120, so I could hardly protect myself from him. And he beat me terribly with his hands and fists, all over, and then he pushed me down. And I was trying to move away from him. I stumbled over a chair leg and then he began to kick me. As I was down on the earth, he began to jump on me and kick me here, on the chest. And I heard a woman saying, "Don't let him. Stop him," something like that. Right after that, the warden approached and to that woman's husband, and he was one of the guards, Milic, and they lifted me and took me to the isolation -- to the solitary confinement room in the new wing of the administrative building, on the ground floor. But Burilo wouldn't give up. He followed us. And even though they were there, he grabbed at me, pushed me, and I hit my head against the wall and I passed out. I came to perhaps two or three hours later. I could hear cars being switched on. I heard voices, noises, and I realised that was the end of the working hours. And I was in solitary confinement. I was lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there and ask you about some of the people whose names you've mentioned. Do you know Burilo's first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not really sure. I think he was Milenko Burilo, called Busi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Milenko Burilo is listed in Exhibit P3 as number 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the woman you said who was saying, "Don't let him," who was she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know her name, but I know she was guard Milic's wife, and she worked there in the coffee shop, made coffee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a Persa Milic listed in Exhibit P3 at number 60, who is a cook, sales assistant, and worked at the farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of the guard Milic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure again. I think he is Milivoj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has a brother called Dragisa. That I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, in fact, a Milivoj Milic listed in Exhibit P3 at number 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- the warden, Mr. Krnojelac, did he actually see Burilo beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that, because he beat -- I mean, it lasted, the beating lasted, and when I got there, I did not see anyone else around except him. So my guess is that that woman, that lady we are talking about, that she came out because she heard what was going on, and I suppose that she came out of the coffee shop, or from some room or other, and I guess that is how her husband arrived and the warden, because I did not see them at that moment; they were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Burilo stop when the warden and the guard Milic arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, stop, he did not. He kept trying to get at me, but they took me towards the solitary confinement. And as I said, he followed us and at some point he caught up, pushed me against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he did that, was the warden also present with Milic, the guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 3.00 and not 2.30, and we'll be sitting until 4.30. We'll now adjourn. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, before the break, you told us that the warden, Milorad Krnojelac, was present when Burilo pushed you up against the wall and you lost consciousness. Do you know whether Burilo ever suffered any consequences of the way he treated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that he was ever punished and that there could have been any consequences. Before that, that Burilo had done so many things and yet he was never punished or sanctioned or was he sent away. On the contrary, those who were tolerant, those guards who - how should I put this - helped, they were sent away from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this incident, did Burilo continue to work as a guard at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you came, regained your consciousness, where did you find yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in that solitary confinement -- in the transit solitary confinement area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which building was that located in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new part of the administration building, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit P6/1. This is a diagram of the ground floor of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us where this cell was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance. This is -- this is where the entrance office is. This is this hallway. This is the place where this incident occurred. And that transit solitary confinement was one of these rooms here. I can't say at this moment which one exactly. I don't think that the drawing is very precise either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed to -- first he pointed, as you come into the entrance of the KP Dom, he turned slightly to the left, and that's where he said this incident occurred. And then the room that he indicated as being the isolation or solitary cell, the transit solitary room, is about the second or third room, counting from the left of the diagram, and also as you would be walking into the KP Dom through the entrance, it would be on your left-hand side as well, and therefore that's the bottom part of the diagram. And he says he's not sure whether it was -- he pointed to what appeared to be the third room or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, is that also the same room that you were in earlier after your interrogation, when you saw the three injured men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. It's the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened to you when you regained consciousness? Did somebody come to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one who came to speak to me was Miro Prodanovic. He opened the door, and stood at the door facing the hall, the entrance office, that duty room, so that he could see who might come up. He said literally, "Zeka, sorry I cursed at you upstairs but please try to understand I barely stayed alive yesterday." And at that moment, I realised that he was the one who stayed back to guard us when Relja Goljanin, head of the metal shop, had gone out of the compound. And then I said, "Well, it doesn't matter, never mind." He went on. He said, "Watch out. They know such and such things." The man who is mentioned here on the list under number 210, "told them all the details concerning your escape. They know everything." Among other things, he had said that, "My relative" - who was a guard there at the time, for one period of time in the camp - "that he conveyed certain pieces of information to you. You know that he was not looked upon kindly even before that. Try to dispel that. They are going to interrogate you tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Miro Prodanovic said this to you, do you know who he was referring to as being the relative of his who was also a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavisa Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you had dealings with Slavisa Prodanovic while you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't really help me any. A few times we stood and talked briefly, a minute or two, and during these encounters he conveyed things to me, like some information that he had come across, like where some of the family members of persons who were detained in the KP Dom with me were. But specifically, whether he had done something for me or helped me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand Miro Prodanovic to mean when he said that Slavisa Prodanovic was not looked upon kindly even before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the aggression started, this conflict, there were people who -- how should I put this? I don't know how to put this. Those who were not in favour of this hard-line wing of the SDS, and allegedly he was one of them, it was sufficient not to be on their side to be an enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the way Slavisa Prodanovic treated the detainees have an effect on his standing among the administration of the KP Dom, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't have any direct contact with us. He was outside, at one of the guard posts outside, and I know that he was strictly forbidden from having contact with us, just like the rest of the guards. They were only supposed to communicate with us officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would the official communications occur? What do you mean by "communicate with you officially"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Carry out orders, do various jobs, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Miro Prodanovic is listed in Exhibit P3 at number 51, and Slavisa Prodanovic is listed in P3 at number 116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what Miro Prodanovic's function in the KP Dom was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know exactly, but he was often in contact with the Serb detainees. That leads me to believe that he was sort of in charge of them, that he was one of their rehabilitation officers or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you react to what Miro Prodanovic said to you? Did you say anything to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say anything to him. When he said, "Sorry that I cursed at you," I said, "Oh, well, never mind. Let go of that now." And then he said what they knew and what they did not know and what they expected of me tomorrow at the interrogation. In an indirect way, he called certain things to my attention so that I would not act rashly and do something stupid and make my position even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else come to the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. Later lots of them started coming in. The warden came, then Relja came, then the guards came, Vlatko one of them. And then the warden came after that too; I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it in order. You said the warden came. Did he come by himself or with other people, and what did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who he came with. This was in front of the door. But he entered my -- office; I almost said "office." He entered the solitary cell. At that moment, I was sitting on the bed, and then the conversation started. First of all, he got a pack of cigarettes out of his pocket. I remember well. It was a Herzegovina brand, without a filter. There was a full pack and we both lit a cigarette. And then he started talking. He said that I had acted foolishly, that I should not have tried to escape, that I was planned for an exchange, that I ruined everything by doing this, that it was very difficult for him and that he was very sorry that this had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his demeanour when he said these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was visibly upset. He was angry. Because what had happened, that is, that I had escaped, that sort of meant that they were not capable of doing their job, that they were not up to the trust that had been vested in them by the tasks that they were assigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your impression of the reason the warden came to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He wanted to have information as to where I had planned to go, how I intended to go. He asked for details, which way I had passed, how I had passed. You see, in my first statements to the policemen who were up there with me, I told them one story and then I told the warden the truth, that is to say, that I got out of the KP Dom and that I crossed the bridge, and the entire route that I took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you lie to the civilian policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say for sure. I couldn't go into all these details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the warden's reaction when you told him how you escaped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what was his reaction? He was angry, he was upset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It didn't last long. Perhaps about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, Relja came, Vlatko, some other guards who I don't know. They threatened me. They said, "See what you've done. Now we are all going to be held accountable." But I knew that nobody would be held accountable. Well, they just had to talk. Then some other guards came, ones I did not know. They tried to mistreat me. Some of them tried to beat me. It wasn't anything very bad. And then they locked up this isolation -- this solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So up until the moment that you've just described when they locked the cell, were guards able to come in as they pleased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described Relja coming in, and also you named Vlatko. When they came in, was the warden still there or had he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that particular detail, whether they were there before or after because I could not register everything. I was still feeling slightly dizzy but I did know that they came. Vlatko asked me, like, "Where are your tools?" As if I had cut the bars and escaped in that way. And I said, "What do you mean, would I have any tools, files? I just walked out through the gate of the construction compound."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when some of the guards came in, that they threatened you. Did they actually beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, until they locked the solitary cell, some of them came to kick me, hit me, threaten me. Later on, they locked the solitary cell so they couldn't get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who locked the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It was somebody who was on duty then, by the gate. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of guards who beat you that -- during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the names of these guards. I knew very few of those guards, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards say what consequences they might suffer as a result of your having escaped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them said, because they were so upset, that others would take it out on them and that, first, when the posse was organised, that they had to run all over the forest that night, and now that they would be sent to the front line and that it's far more difficult for them to go there than to be the guards on duty at the KP Dom. That's what one of them was saying to me, one who tried to break the door down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him. That was Mara, Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think he knew his real name himself. Everybody called him Mara. I think Milomir was his real name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, on Exhibit P3 at number 102, there is a Milomir Maric listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you spend that night, Mr. Zekovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I had other visitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who visited you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was already evening. It must have been 7.00 or even past 7.00 when the door of the solitary confinement cell was unlocked and in came Savo Todovic. He said that I should get out, and he took me to the office by the entrance. That's where I found Boro Ivanovic and someone else. They called him Mandic when they talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Boro Ivanovic? You mentioned him earlier in your testimony but could you remind us who he is? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boro Ivanovic, member of the Crisis Staff, a teacher in the elementary school in Godijeno, I think, Godijeno Dragocaje. He came very often. He was in front of the KP Dom often. And then he was going to Montenegro with Savo Todovic to wait for me at 210's place, because he had said that I would stop at that man's place and that I would rest perhaps for a day, get some food, and that then I would continue my journey to Montenegro, towards Previla. So they had set up an ambush for me there. And then when they received information, somehow, that I was caught, they came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Boro Ivanovic in a military uniform or civilian clothes when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They changed these uniforms very often. Military, different kinds, civilian. It was very hard to know. They were not the same all the time. It was sort of like a military jacket, that's what he wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. However, he was also there the next day during the interrogation, so I assumed that he was someone from the military police, or rather, that he was a bit higher up. Perhaps he was from somewhere else, maybe even from Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Boro Ivanovic say to you when Todovic brought you to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, Savo Todovic started beating me. He ordered me to sit in a chair by the entrance, and then he grabbed me this way and started banging me against the wall. And then at one moment, he found some kind of chains, some thick chains, and then he started beating me with those chains. But that wasn't that bad. It's not that I fainted. At one moment, you get this feeling that you should react. I had similar situations before. I turned to Boro and I said, "If we are going to talk like human beings, we are going to talk. If we are going to talk like dogs, we are not going to talk at all." Boro spoke to Savo and said, "Okay, stop that." And then Boro addressed me. He said, "Listen, Zeka, we sent information to the command, saying that you were killed during your attempted escape. It depends on what you say tomorrow, whether that piece of information will be confirmed or whether it will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, the witness said that Boro Ivanovic said that from the military command -- that from the military command, they had said that he was killed during his attempted escape, whereas in line 75 it says only "command."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you say he added the word "military" to it, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you could clear that up, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that "from" the military command they sent word. Not "to" the military command but "from" the military command. That was my understanding of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we will get it cleared up directly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic we will have to go through exactly what Boro Ivanovic said to you again. It may have been a translation error but we will need to hear it again. What did he tell you about information about your escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the command, I cannot say now whether it's military or civilian or police or the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I have to react if you allow me to. We speak the same language and I know what I heard. I would ask kindly to listen to the tape later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You will have every opportunity in cross-examination to ask questions about this, but the Prosecution is permitted to ask the witness to repeat it, to see what he intended to say. If it turns out to be something different from what you heard, we can have the tape played. But the Prosecution is allowed to have this cleared up. You've raised the question as to the accuracy of the translation. If I may say so, your interpretation of it doesn't fit into the sentence that the witness was using. But nevertheless, it's fair enough. It should be cleared up. But at the moment, the Prosecution can attempt to clear up. Now, will you please let them do that? Yes, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic, we'll have to go through it again, and just pay special attention to where the information was coming from and whether you know the nature of the command. What did Boro Ivanovic tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about what kind of command it was and who it was and what that was, so I cannot say whether it's a military command, whether it's the Crisis Staff, whether it's the civilian police, or whether it's the administration of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say that the information about your having died during the escape came from or was sent to this command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he said, "We from the command." I don't know who he was referring to, the administration or whoever. I could not have checked that. I could not have asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us what he told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We from the command have sent information that you were killed during your attempted escape, and now it depends on what you say in your statement tomorrow whether this information will be confirmed or whether it will be denied."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you react or did he say anything further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not react at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Savo Todovic do anything at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then it was said that I should be taken to the solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you spend the night, then, in solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I spent the whole night in solitary confinement with my hands handcuffed and my legs tied to a metal ring in the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a bed in that room. Were you able to sleep on the bed or did you have to lie on the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The bed was on the other end of the room. I was not allowed to take either the pillow that was there or the blanket. I was on the floor. It's not concrete; it's parquet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, first a guard came to have a look at me and then I asked him if I could go to the toilet, but he refused. Then Savo Todovic turned up in the doorway, and I asked him to go to the toilet and he allowed me to do it. And then they took me to an office on the ground floor again, but on the other side of the passage, to interrogate me there. And there was an entire commission there. There were three police inspectors: Savo Todovic, Boro Ivanovic, that Mandic was there, and I think one or two more were also present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said the three -- you said there were three police inspectors. Did you mean to say that Todovic, Ivanovic and Mandic were those three, or were there three police inspectors in addition to the three you named?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those three were from the civilian police, other people, other than those three, who had already been in the camp and conducted interrogations: Starovic, Vladicic, and Janjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who conducted the interrogation? Who asked you questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inspector Vladicic and Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kinds of questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They simply said, "We know. We have all the information, but this is a procedure. You have to tell us the whole story, from the first day that you were brought to the camp, right up to this moment," where I was, what I did, where I moved about, who I communicated with, and all that I knew about the plans or intentions of other camp inmates, and which of the staff working in the compound, in the KP Dom, who were favourable to us, who did favours to us, who we could cooperate with -- who were cooperative, rather. That is what they wanted to know: who were we getting information from. And I said that when I went to work outside, that I then came across people that I knew from before, and I therefore asked them questions I wanted to know, and that in the hospital I met Dejan Malisa and I asked him some questions, because he was close with my brother and he told me that my brother called him from Germany. Then I told them that I also came across other people and also asked them for information, and they told me about other prisoners, that their families were in Skopje, in Sweden, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that completely the truth? Did you answer that question truthfully or did you withhold information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because the information that they wanted to get from me, actually, I obtained from Slavisa Prodanovic, for instance, about my brother and other things, and I was told that by my friend, who is number 210 in the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you protect Slavisa Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really pinpoint the reason. I simply thought that man was in some trouble before, so I shouldn't cause any more trouble for him with my statements. I didn't want to make it worse for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other things did the inspectors and others during that interrogation ask you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Savo asked me about the kind of conversations in the room we had, and they also wanted to know -- they really wanted to know what we knew, what we talked about, did we know who he was, what he was, who was the warden, and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you answer Todovic's questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Either. Well, to begin with -- to begin with, I couldn't really tell them anything of any interest, none of the things that they wanted to hear. And it is quite true that we did have some information about what had been done and what crimes had been committed. Yes, we knew all that. And I then resorted to an incident which had happened in 1992 to try to say that I didn't know anything that was going on in the room, that they all kept their distance from me and therefore were not communicating with me, and that I was isolated, and it worked. And that incident had to do with the last radio that we had, which I have already mentioned. And Stela, from Miljevina, was the one who snitched on me because of that radio. And when Savo said, "You can't say that you don't know what you're talking about in the room, because you've been together so long that you must know everything and you must tell me all that," and I told him, "I don't know, because since the incident with the transistor last year, everybody in the room believed that I was responsible for it, that it was through some fault of mine that that radio had been seized and that it was because of that that very many people were beaten and suffered greatly. And then I saw the inspectors casting looks at one another. They evidently were in the dark about that incident. And I didn't think it was such an important affair that everybody had to know about it. And that is how I somehow managed to avoid telling them about all these details. I mean, I didn't want to tell them. And then Savo asked me -- first he affirmed that he knew that some guards were doing favours to us and good deeds, that they brought us cigarettes or things like that, and he said, "Well, which one is the best? Which one is the most cooperative?" And I said, "There aren't such. They don't exist." "What do you mean, they don't exist?" I said, "Well, they don't exist. Were there such a man in the camp compound, I would have agreed with him to have a car wait for me when I got to the road and I would be in Montenegro half an hour later, rather than have to look where is the patrol, shall I swim across the Drina, where are the mine fields, and so on and so forth," and they seemed satisfied with that answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated during that interrogation? Did anybody beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not beat me during the interrogation. When I gave them the answer that I've told you about, the one called Mandic jumped up and said, "Give him to me. Wait till I get him into my hands, and then he'll talk," and then they took me out into the passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when they took you out to the passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent about ten minutes outside, and then they brought me back into the office and they kept their silence for a long time. And then they said - and it was this inspector Vladicic and Savo were the ones who spoke - and they said, "Well, this time this is how this matter ends, but in the future, if we suspect anything, that will be the end of you. So just scram." And I went back to that room, solitary confinement room, where I had spent the previous night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a time that same day when the other detainees from the working group were lined up and you were also brought up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the afternoon. I don't know if it was 3.00 or 4.00 in the afternoon; thereabouts. I was taken out of this solitary confinement and taken into the camp courtyard. And the prisoners, or rather, the camp inmates were all lined up in the playground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- they were lined up. On one side were the camp inmates who were lined up, and on the other side were the staff of the KP Dom, almost all the guards. There was Savo, there was the warden, and Savo delivered a speech. "Well, you see this is yet another proof that the borders of the Republika Srpska are impenetrable, that not even a bird can fly across. And had we killed him, we would have brought him here to show him to you as a warning so that nobody ever tries this again. And because you were not sufficiently alert because they permitted" -- listen, what nonsense, that they allowed me to escape. And he ordered -- he punished all of the camp inmates. He said, "As of today, your food rations will be cut down by 50 per cent." It was insufficient even before. Another 50 per cent. He forbid to go to work. He forbid medical examinations. He forbid -- ordered the search of all the rooms where the camp inmates were kept, and that all their things be seized. Meanwhile some people had obtained something, we have got some books and we read them and some old newspapers. So that everything was taken away on that occasion, and that includes medicines. And at some point, a camp inmate stepped forward, a teacher. He stepped forward and he asked when he heard do we -- when it was said that everything that did not belong to us had to be returned. So he asked, "And what about these clothes?" What he had was convicts' clothes. And the answer was, "No, no, no, no, no, because it is very becoming." And then he ordered to take me to place me in solitary confinement and said, "And mind what kind of treatment he gets now." So I was searched at the entrance into solitary confinement and locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Savo Todovic say anything about whether guards would be punished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not hear him say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the warden present throughout this speech that Todovic gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. He was right next to him, with his hands behind his back, and kept nodding, nodding his head in approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought before the other detainees and prison staff at this time, what physical condition were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I could barely walk. There were no visible traces, not on my face, but everything hurt, because Burilo had beat me very badly for two months. After that, I could not raise my arms. This shoulder is still dysfunctional to this day and I have terrible problems with my legs and feet because I was also badly beaten down there. I could barely stand, and everybody could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken away to the solitary cell, where was that cell located? Was it the transit cell that you were in earlier or was it a different one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was a solitary confinement cell which existed already in the former prison, the upper row of solitary cells which were made when we were detained in the camp, in the metal shop, true -- before I started to work there, they had already finished them, those solitary cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, were these solitary cells inside the metal shop? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The staff in the metal shop built built-in metal doors and metal grids above the door, metal bars above the door, because those solitary cells had not been completed at the time the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'll have the witness take a look at Exhibit P6/2 and see if he can indicate to us where he was taken, the solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not an accurate drawing. In this row, there are two rows of solitary cells. One enters here and this is a large hallway and then you enter the lower row of solitary cells and on the upper side, into the upper row of solitary cells. And the passage is by the wall. And you go up the stairs. Downstairs, I don't know the outlay because I was not kept there. But these are the new solitary cells which were completed after people were detained in the camp. They were begun before the detention. They had begun building them before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when they were completed or when those metal doors were made by the detainees? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Metal doors for these cells were completed and mounted by men in the metal shop before I went to work there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness is indicating the solitary confinement cells which photographs we've seen previously, and that would be located in the second building of the prisoners' quarters on the first -- on the ground floor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in that cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twenty-eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Either while you were brought there or while you were inside that cell, did anybody beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me. The first evening, they took me out of the solitary cell, took off the handcuffs off my hands, and beat me. And the same thing happened the next evening. But it wasn't all that bad, and when I say "all that bad," I mean I did not faint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guards on duty that night. I recognised one. And the second time it was people I knew, Milutinovic from Jelec, Zoran Matovic from Josanica, and one Ristanovic; I think his first name was Momo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that they took your handcuffs off. Were you able to defend yourself when they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's a little -- well, I could try to defend myself but it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you try to defend yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose try to dodge the blows, try to move away or something like that, but they just corner you and you can't get away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten by individual guards or by groups of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion, not all of them beat me. Two took part in that and one just stood and watched. Zoran Matovic just stood and watched. And at some point -- I already told you, time comes when you have to react and it seems to you that it's the right moment. And when this guard Ristanovic said that he'd heard that he knew that I had worked for UNIS before that, that I was a bad man, that I persecuted Serbs, I said that that was not right, and that the truth was quite the contrary, that I had very many friends whom I helped and one of them was this Matovic's relative. And some 15 or 20 days before the war broke out, I donated blood for his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything while they were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing specific, nothing definite, except that that Ristanovic said that he had heard that I was a bad man, that I persecuted Serbs at a place I worked at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Momcilo Ristanovic is listed in Exhibit P3 at number 41, and Milutinovic is listed at P3 at number 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any guards beat you when they brought you food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Once Predrag Stefanovic, called Predo, brought my supper. I used to know him before the war, and he spent hundreds of nights with me at various parties or outings, excursions. So he brought this food and said, "Well, and this is for me," and started kicking me. And he was wearing those army boots at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Predrag Stefanovic is listed on P3 at number 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you taken out of solitary confinement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
