utterances.text: You mean when I left it completely? Because they took me out several times. They took me out to beat me twice. And on one occasion, I don't know when it was, in the morning, around 9.00 or 10.00, or perhaps it could have been noon, I'm not sure because I had lost all sense of time, I was taken out into the reception room at the entrance into the building, and Savo Todovic interrogated me there again. And they had also taken off the handcuffs because I -- they never took handcuffs off me, and that is how I spent seven days on just bare concrete, nothing else. And then Savo Todovic began to question me about some details which I had mentioned during my statement about the escape. And he pointed out that he was doing it as an expert, as a psychologist, or rather, literally he said, "I'm doing it as your brother would do," because my brother is a psychologist. And I said, "My brother would never do this." And then he told me that I didn't know my manners. And he supposedly wanted to clarify, to shed more -- to understand better my mind-set, my -- the way of thinking, the way I conceived my escape so as to allegedly use this in his future work. And when I told him in that village after I had escaped and crossed that bridge and coming out of a forest, when I had seen two girls of five, six years old, and returned into the forest, because I was afraid they -- that they would see me, and he said, "Well, did it occur to you, for instance, to kidnap them and then blackmail us?" Which was nonsense. And I said, "I'm not a criminal. My girls are that age and it is because of them that I escaped from this hell, hoping that I would find them and see them again. And you say that I could kidnap some little girls? Come."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Savo Todovic took you out to interrogate you, did he physically mistreat you? Did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that time, he did not beat me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you were taken out twice and beaten. Where were you taken on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the solitary cell into the hallway in front of the solitary cells. It's also like a hall, like a room. And there are doors leading from it to the upper and the lower row of solitary cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken -- you said you were in the solitary cell for 28 days. How were you finally released from the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day before I was released from the solitary cell, I was -- we were taken to have a bath. That is the officer who escorted us, he ordered me, because of course I knew the layout of the compound, to go there with our heads down, not to look left or right, and he ordered us to go and have the bath and he stayed in front of the building. So I immediately assumed that the Red Cross would be -- were on their way. And that day, a camp inmate, Mujo Dudic, called Kuja, he swept the rooms in the building and he also swept those rooms which were solitary confinement cells. That is not the solitary cells but the passageway. And he was -- as he was passing by my cell, I called out to him and said, "What's the matter?" And he said, "Red Cross will be here tomorrow." And the next morning I asked the duty officer to be taken to meet Rasevic, to request that I be released or to go to see the warden. That's what I said. And he answered, "Right, I will see about it." And he returned half an hour later and told me to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to return to one detail about your confinement in the solitary cell. Were you handcuffed the entire time when you were inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was handcuffed for about seven days. Well, perhaps it was six and a half or seven and a half. I wouldn't really know. Listen, I was so badly beaten up, on the concrete, I weighed less than 50 -- I had less than 50 kilograms in me, and I couldn't sleep normally. At times I thought it was night at times that it was daytime. A couple of days later, I somehow managed to recover my sense of time on the basis of outside sounds, because above me on the first floor of the same building, there were detained Serbs, and they listened to the news and that was how I could figure out what time of the day it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two times that you were taken out and beaten, was that during those seven days when you were handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were the first two days. Those were the first two days. And then the next day after that, Savo asked me -- after this other case, Savo asked me, when he was interrogating me, "Did anybody beat you?" And I said, "Yes." And he said, "Who?" And I said, "You know full well who was on duty." And that's how the conversation ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to when Mitar Rasevic said that you should get ready and you were brought out of the room. Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who said that. I just asked to go to see the warden or Mitar Rasevic, to talk to them. I wanted to ask them to let me go. And then this guard came and then I was released, and then we went from the solitary confinement cells upstairs, to Room 18. And now the condition that I was in is best illustrated by the fact that I could barely walk upstairs. I had to cling to the railing. And they brought me to this room were Muhamed was, the one we had already discussed in this isolation room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his last name, just so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muhamed Ahmetkadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time there were also five Croats in Room 18; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in -- no, not in that room. They were on the other side of that sleeping area, because that sleeping area had four rooms, two big ones and two small ones. In one big room were the Croats, and in another small room, on the upper side, that's where Muhamed was by himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to have contact with those Croats also kept in Room 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Nobody had forbidden it specifically, but we moved about in there and we would meet. However, only two talked; three never did. Muhamed told those two what was going on. Usually with persons from such rooms, what usually happened to them, that they would take them away and they would go missing. And they told me that they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn why those Croats were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They told me. They were taken prisoner somewhere at the front line. But very soon, a few days later, the attitude of the guards towards them changed drastically. They came and talked to them. They brought them cigarettes. They brought them lots of food. They talked to them openly, like all the conflicts between the Serbs and the Croats had been worked out and now what is left is that they finish off the Muslims together, and that now at various delineation lines the Serbs and Croats were playing soccer together, that everything has been resolved. And very soon, a few days after that, they took them away. Mitar Rasevic came to the room, into their room, and said that they could go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these Croats in military uniform? Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had some kind of civilian uniforms on, but they were soldiers, because they were taken prisoner as soldiers. Among them was a man without a leg. He had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the Serb guards came and that their attitude changed drastically. Did their attitude toward you and Mr. Ahmetkadic change as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I cannot say anything. Once, one guard gave me a cigarette, both to me and to Muhamed, and he said, "You should thank certain people for having stayed alive." And I insisted that he tell me who these people are, and he didn't want to say. He said, "You'll find out when the time comes."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever find out who he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never found out. But I heard something similar to that in the transit solitary cell, when I was brought in there after my attempted escape, when the door of the solitary cell was locked. I heard something similar to that. They tried to break down the door to beat me, and one of them said that he would stab me with a knife, that he wouldn't kill me but that I would bleed for three days and that then I would die. And then I said, "Mara, why?" And he was yelling, hollering. He said, "What do you mean, why? Because we all got into trouble because of you. We all had problems." And there were also some there who were cursing at me, and somebody was saying from the gate - and I heard that with perfect clarity - somebody said, "You can't do anything to him. He's been registered with the Red Cross and he is protected by --" and I didn't hear the name. So I think that is the fact that I should thank for having stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you registered with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The papers that I got from the International Red Cross say that this was the end of August. I don't know exactly. Perhaps I may be wrong. That is to say that I was registered from August and that I was detained from August. That was my understanding. But I was actually detained on the 20th of May, and allegedly this list was given to the Red Cross by the administration of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were listed as registered in August. Was that August 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if you were registered in August of 1992? Did you give the Red Cross your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not give my name. I didn't have any contact. I was not in touch with them at all. They got this list from someone, and it was not a complete list. It was not complete, no, no, not for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why the attitude of the Serb guards toward the Croat soldiers changed so drastically; what prompted that change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I assumed then was confirmed by what happened afterwards. All of this was part of a well-elaborated strategy of an approach both vis-a-vis the International Community and the situation within Bosnia. It was necessary to create a situation which would lead everyone to believe that the Muslims are to be blamed for everything and that everybody could find a common tongue except for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you ever learn why, in particular, at that moment their attitude changed? Did something happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their political leaderships then formulated some joint objectives. There was a conflict that broke out then on the Croat side, and they cooperated on the front line through joint efforts and they were helped considerably by the Serbs as well - that is what we heard - and that they had intended to divide up the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina between themselves, and that if a sliver of land were to remain, that the Muslims could keep that, but that the Serbs and the Croats would divide between themselves the largest part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was in conversations with various guards who you could talk to. And we said that perhaps that would not be possible, that the International Community would intervene, especially when we heard that the Security Council had proclaimed those safe areas. They just laughed at that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Room 18 at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a long time. About a month, over a month. And then, one morning, they called Muhamed Ahmetkadic to go to the furniture factory, because he was a tailor in addition to being a driver, and I remained on my own. A few hours, later a guard came and said that Savo Todovic asked me to come out in the yard, and I went out. Then he asked me, a bit cheekily, "What are we going to do with you?" And I said, "Well, my proposal is that we write a request to the administration," since I had almost reached the border and I had almost gotten free and reached my children, that they should release me. And he said, "You are really cheeky. Get lost. Go back to work." And then he took me to where I worked. He handed me over to the foreman there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this at the metal shop or did you begin working at the furniture factory then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The furniture factory within the compound of the prison, whereas the metal shop is outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time when you were in the solitary cell and then in Room 18, did the management of the KP Dom change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know the exact date. I can't say specifically right now, but a new warden came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about that from the other inmates who had more information, who could move about. And then when I started working at the furniture factory, on the second or the third day, this new warden came, Sekulovic, and Radojica Tesevic, who was director of the economic unit before the war, but for a long time he had been eliminated by the SDS because they did not look upon him favourably. And they talked to us quite nicely. The food got better, which was very, very important for us. This new warden and Radojica Tesevic said that they would do whatever they could, whatever was within their powers to improve our status. They primarily meant our stay there and food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Radojica Tesevic was eliminated by the SDS because they did not look upon him favourably. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant what I know, that Radojica Tesevic and his brother, who hanged himself, were not extremists and did not approve of what the extremists were doing in Foca. Radojica Tesevic, for a long time, was an external guard by the bridge on the banks of the Drina River, a plain guard with a rifle. He did not have access to the indoor facilities at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this after he was taken away from his previous job as warden that he became an ordinary guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand your question exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I misspoke. You said in your previous answer that Radojica Tesevic was director of the economic unit before the war. Was he demoted to being a guard because of what you said, that he was not an extremist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Radojica Tesevic is listed on P3 at number 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what function he had under the new administration with the new warden, Sekulovic? What was Tesevic's function? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say exactly, and I cannot exactly describe his job and his duties, but according to what we found out, he became director of the economic unit. I don't know whether that referred to the entire production programme, that is to say, both the furniture factory and the farm. That I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While Milorad Krnojelac was warden, who was the director of the economic unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Sekulovic and Tesevic promised that things would improve. Did they improve? You mention the food already. Did anything else improve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. The visits of the Red Cross became more regular. Then also we were allowed to heat water within the camp compound. In front of the kitchen there was a big caldron that was heated, and people could take hot water for doing their washing or for taking baths, although there were still some problems with some guards who did not allow that. But this was arbitrariness. On one occasion I was beaten by Predrag Stefanovic, nicknamed Predo, because I tried to take some of that water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the disappearances that you discussed earlier in your testimony continue after the new warden came in, where people were taken out for exchange and then disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. People were not taken out en masse any more, killed, and people weren't taken out for interrogations. Although these interrogations had stopped also towards the end of the term of this warden here, but the attitude towards us, our treatment, the climate in general, changed a lot, not only of the new warden and of Radojica Tesevic, but also generally speaking; the staff, the guards, they were all softer and more pleasant. In that period, it already would happen that our rooms would not be locked, that we could actually visit each other, we who would go out to work and those who did not go out to work, and then they would let us go and have lunch or dinner together. In the autumn of 1993, the Red Cross brought us a furnace, so we were allowed to use it in the room, although we could have made that kind of a furnace in the metal workshop, too. I and my comrade from the shop, number 210, we had made dozens of such furnaces for the front lines, for the military. We could have made some for us as well but the administration didn't allow that. We spent the winter of 1992-93 without any heating at all. We talked about that situation, the situation in the camp, very little. I thought that we should go back to that to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several witnesses have already discussed the conditions and that's why we did not focus on that in your testimony. Did the attitude of Savo Todovic change after the new warden Sekulovic started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There is no way you could say that. He was still arrogant, impudent. I stopped working at the furniture factory in mid-December, 1993. I worked there for about three, three and a half months. One day, a guard came and said, "Go to the room and don't go out again until we call you." I thought that the next day, I would go to the mine to work, to the brown coal mine where our people started going to work. However, a day had gone by, two days, five days, and nobody called me. Only later, I found out from another guard that Savo Todovic withdrew me from work because he was afraid that I might try to escape again and reach some kind of agreement to that effect, because at that time two Serbs had escaped from prison and he had probably assumed that I would reach some kind of agreement with someone. All winter, I was in the room. I didn't go out to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the attitude -- or, rather, were guards like Burilo permitted to beat people after the change of administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that that didn't take place that much any more. There were a few minor incidents of this nature but not even close to what had happened before. Burilo slapped Zanda in the face a few times. Zanda was being a bit perky, whatever, but no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described at -- toward the beginning of your testimony that you worked in the brown coal mine towards the end of your detention. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I don't know the exact date but I worked from April until the last day I was in the camp. One day, in the spring of 1994, there were quite a few people who could not go to work. You should know that, by then, we had been in camp for two years. The food was very bad. Many people had been abused, mistreated. Lots of people were sick. However, they needed someone to work. One day, Savo was revolted because he heard that a lot of people were sick and could not go to work. He called all of us to come outside. We went out and then he said, "You go to the farm, you go to the furniture factory. Zeka, to the mine."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 6th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for the fact that you were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think -- I think that it is primarily due to the International Red Cross. An exchange had been agreed upon before, once, in the autumn of 1993. I can't say exactly whether it was in October or November. Just after their visit, the Red Cross came back again soon. We were more than surprised. They said that some kind of an agreement had been reached on exchanges. They even carried out a poll, some kind of poll. They gave us questionnaires so that people could say where they wanted to go, and they said that it was highly likely that something would happen within a few days or perhaps within two weeks. However, they never came. Later, we found out that this exchange had been stopped by the administration of the KP Dom, or rather the people whom this did not suit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of the time that you spent in KP Dom, you mentioned you have problems with your arm still. Can you explain or describe other physical things that you suffer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have injuries on my feet. It's not that I can't move, but I have problems. Once when I worked in the mine, I hurt my knee. It was badly swollen and it was all black. I went to the male nurse within the compound where there was a prison hospital before. When he saw it, he was appalled. A lady doctor used to come from the health centre. When she saw the condition I was in, she said that it was impossible for me to go to work but that I had to get a drip as soon as possible, and that I needed, I can't say exactly how many now, five to seven. But the next day, I did not go to work. The guard from the gate came with a baton and he forced me to go. He said, "I'm going to give you a drip. I'm going to give you sick leave. Off you go to work." So I had to go. It was more than terrible, because I could not walk, and you had to work. And this was heavy, physical labour. As we entered the mine, we would have to carry big logs on our backs. Logs that were used within the mine then. So at some moments, I even contemplated suicide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lose weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In that period in particular, when I got out of the solitary cell. Before the war, I weighed 83, 84, 85 kilograms. I was always healthy. I was a sportsman all my life. My weight had dropped to about 50 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one or two more questions but I see it's 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sure he will be required for some time for cross-examination. Sir, we are resuming again on Monday, the 12th of March, so we will have you back to complete your evidence then. You may leave now. There is a few matters I have to raise with counsel before we depart, but you may leave the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I propose to ask the languages section to check the translation. Perhaps a number of different of the interpreters could look at it independently, at page 75, lines 21 to 24 of today's LiveNote, and then that can be dealt with when we resume. Mr. Bakrac, I have to say this, though: I understand you feel that because you speak the same language you can debate these matters, but we do have very expert interpreters here in court. I am always prepared to accept that they can make an error because of the speed at which they have to do the interpreting. You may ask for something to be checked, but you cannot prevent the Prosecution from following up something which you've raised. You will get every opportunity, when you get a checked translation to take it up in cross-examination, but I do hope that you will not attempt to interfere with the Prosecution's case in that way again. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was waiting for the interpretation, and I see that you're moving on to another subject, but I cannot but apologise to the Prosecutors. Perhaps I reacted impulsively at that moment. And I hope that the Prosecution won't hold this against me or that you won't hold it against me. Really, there was no ill intention involved. I react impulsively because I really heard him say that. That's what I heard. I mean, you know, that's the reason why I reacted impulsively, nothing else. And I was looking at the transcript and I saw that this did not reflect in the transcript. I reacted immediately at the same moment without having counted to ten and thought about it a bit more. I thought that after that, perhaps it would have been too late. I do apologise once again to my distinguished colleagues from the Prosecution, and to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps if I may tell you something as an old person in the law, I never ceased to be amazed at the end of a cross-examination that I had conducted, when I thought that I had received the most amazing concessions from a witness, and I looked at the transcript later. You do sometimes hear what you want to hear, and it doesn't always turn out to be what was in fact said. And that is where there have been no problems with translations. However, we are not going to hold it against you in any way, but I just wanted to make it clear that whilst you are entitled to suggest that the translation that is shown in the transcript is wrong, that's enough. It will be checked. But you must not, perhaps, be so impulsive about trying to interfere with the Prosecution's examination in chief. We certainly won't hold it against you. Well, now, we do apologise. The Trial Chamber feels very badly that we are not sitting next week. However, I am sure that both sides are absolutely delighted that we are not, seeing that both sides attempted to get a longer break than we were prepared to give them. So both sides have in fact won the argument through default. We will resume again on Monday, the 12th of March, at 9.30, I hope in one of the bigger courtrooms. We shall see you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
